metadata.summary: This evidence-based guideline addresses urethral intermittent catheterisation and intermittent urethral dilatation in adults. It covers indications, contraindications, catheter and technique selection, procedures, complications, infection prevention, patient and caregiver education, follow-up, and quality-of-life considerations. Its recommendations support clinical judgement and local protocols rather than replacing individualised decisions.

conditions_covered: neurogenic or non-neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction
target_population: Adults with bladder dysfunction who need intermittent catheterisation, whether once or long-term
Patients and caregivers learning or performing intermittent catheterisation
Nurses and other healthcare professionals assessed as competent in intermittent catheterisation procedures

toxicities.incidence: The reported incidence attributed to IC is in the region of 2.6 and 2.7 per person per year. The 1-year incidence of UTI was 62% to 77% among IC users with a neurogenic disorder and 38% to 42% among users with a non-neurogenic disorder. Lamin and colleagues reported symptomatic CAUTI in 10–15% of IC users. Within the first year of starting IC, Welk and colleagues reported CAUTI in 54.9% of users with a neurogenic disorder versus 38.9% of users with a non-neurogenic disorder; hospitalisation for CAUTI in 11.3% versus 4.0%; and ≥ 3 CAUTIs in 17% versus 9.6%, respectively.
recognition: The guideline associates UTI with urinary symptoms such as dysuria and fever alongside bacteriuria or funguria and a count of > 103 CFU/ml.

Symptoms described in the patient checklist include pain or burning during urination, frequency or urgency, strong-smelling or cloudy urine, blood in urine, fever, chills and flu-like symptoms. Confusion, agitation or delirium may occur in older adults, especially those with underlying conditions.
A higher residual urine volume at catheterisation is associated with more symptomatic infections.

management.severity: Symptoms suggesting UTI in an IC user
management.actions: Perform urinalysis or obtain a urine specimen for culture. Treat symptomatic UTI; do not treat an abnormal urine test in the absence of symptoms.

prevention: Preferably keep bladder volume from exceeding 400–500 ml and assess whether catheterisation frequency needs adjustment.

Use a hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheter; evidence cited by the guideline also indicates a significant reduction in symptomatic CAUTI with ready-to-use catheters combined with a non-touch technique.
Follow hand-hygiene protocols and teach patients and caregivers hand hygiene.
Assess fluid needs individually and encourage intake sufficient to produce at least 1200 ml of urine per day.
Use a sterile single-use catheter to prevent cross-contamination in clinical, rehabilitation and long-term care settings.

toxicities.incidence: Lamin and colleagues reported asymptomatic bacteriuria in 50% of IC users. The guideline reports acquisition of bacteriuria at 1–3% per catheterisation and states that almost all patients have bacteriuria by the end of the third week.
recognition: A positive urine culture without symptoms defines asymptomatic bacteriuria.
For urine obtained with an in-and-out catheter, > 100 colony-forming units (CFU)/ml is consistent with bacteriuria.

management.actions: Do not treat it; the guideline limits treatment in IC users to symptomatic UTI because antibiotics carry risks of resistance and adverse effects.

toxicities.incidence: Håkansson and colleagues reported < 1% per patient per year among patients with neurogenic or non-neurogenic bladder.

In a retrospective study over 17 years (n=140), Ku et al. reported epididymo-orchitis in 27.9% of people with spinal cord injury; it occurred significantly more often among CIC users than among users of indwelling urethral catheterisation.
recognition: Acute epididymitis presents with pain, swelling and increased temperature of the epididymis; the testis and scrotal skin may also be involved.

toxicities.incidence: Singh et al. and Wyndaele reported an incidence of 1–20% in spinal cord injury patients using IC.
recognition: Urethral inflammation usually presents with LUTS and may have an infectious or non-infectious origin.
Acute bacterial prostatitis generally begins abruptly with voiding symptoms and distressing, poorly localised pain, often accompanied by malaise and fever.
Prostatitis can contribute to recurrent UTI.

toxicities.incidence: Håkansson and colleagues reported bleeding at a frequency of 2.2% per year.
recognition: Urethral bleeding can appear as blood in the urine or on the catheter and is seen more frequently when a patient begins IC.
Microscopic haematuria is three or more red blood cells per high-power field (RBC/HPF) on urine microscopy. Visible haematuria may occur from a concentration as low as 1 ml blood per litre of urine.
Mucosal injury can have later consequences, including urethral stricture or infection of the urethral mucosa.

management.actions: Review catheter size and tip, insertion technique, and catheter material, coating and lubrication.

management.severity: Bleeding or difficulty during catheter insertion
management.actions: Review technique, lubrication and catheter characteristics; check for constipation. If needed, consider urethral calibration, urethral X-ray diagnostics or cystoscopy. Do not force insertion when it is difficult.

prevention: Use hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheters for IC; these significantly reduce microscopic haematuria. The guideline does not identify evidence that hydrophilic catheters reduce gross haematuria.
Use lubrication, either incorporated into the catheter or applied externally, to reduce trauma; lubricate non-coated catheters in both women and men.
Select a catheter large enough for free drainage while limiting urethral injury.

toxicities.incidence: A scoping review by Engberg et al. reported 2.2–9% annually, while noting limited research on prevalence and intervention.
recognition: The catheter or another instrument passes through the urethral wall rather than following the urethral lumen.
The catheter may preferentially enter the false passage, leaving the patient unable to continue IC.
prevention: Do not use force when catheter insertion is difficult.

toxicities.incidence: The guideline estimates urethral stricture at about 0.1–1% in women versus 4.2–25% in men and states that occurrence in men increases with time. In a review by Liao et al., incidence was 3.1% with hydrophilic catheters versus 11.5% with nonhydrophilic catheters.
recognition: Urethral narrowing may cause urinary symptoms, obstruction and incomplete emptying.
In men, an anterior urethral stricture involves fibrosis and scarring of the urethral mucosa and surrounding spongiosus tissue.
toxicities.grading: European Association of Urology classification according to degree of urethral narrowing: category 0, normal urethra on imaging; category 1, subclinical strictures with narrowing but ≥ 16 Fr, Low; category 2, low-grade strictures, 11–15 Fr; category 3, high-grade or flow-significant strictures, 4–10 Fr, High; category 4, nearly obliterative strictures, 1–3 Fr; category 5, obliterative strictures with no urethral lumen (0 Fr).

management.actions: Intermittent urethral dilatation is an established palliative option. The guideline states that it can reduce recurrence up to 68%.

management.severity: Stricture for which reconstruction is not possible or repair has failed

prevention: Use hydrophilic-coated catheters to prevent urethral strictures.

toxicities.incidence: Described as a rare complication, with only a few case series reported in the ‘90s.
recognition: Narrowing of the urethral opening can impair voiding and cause incomplete bladder emptying when significant.

management.actions: A meatal dilator or female-length catheter can be used for a male meatal stricture.

toxicities.incidence: Described as rare, with sporadic reports involving augmented bladders at the anastomotic site.
Described as extremely rare and reported more often in children.
recognition: The catheter coils around itself and its end passes through the coils.
prevention: Select the catheter carefully and ensure understanding of urethral anatomy and safe catheter insertion lengths.

toxicities.incidence: Bartel et al. reported bladder stones in 2% of spinal cord injury patients using IC, versus 11% using suprapubic catheters and 6.6% using indwelling catheters. Their mean period to stone development was ~10 years, and time to recurrence was 26 months.
recognition: The guideline links increased risk to recurrent UTI with ureaseproducing organisms, incomplete bladder emptying, permanent catheters, immobilisation and hypercalciuria.

Long-term IC is associated with increased bladder calculus formation in children and adults, with higher risk when IC is performed through a Mitrofanoff procedure; introduced pubic hair can serve as a nidus.

Ecer et al. reported an association with IC in patients with neurogenic bladder compared with patients not using IC; the study identified CAUTI and prostatitis as the most important factors increasing prostate calculus frequency.
Pain can occur during or after insertion or removal, or in connection with bladder spasm or UTI.
Incomplete pelvic-floor relaxation, postmenopausal mucosal atrophy and insufficient lubrication can make insertion or removal painful.
Johansson et al. reported significantly more burning and pain with a hydrophilic PVC catheter than with a PVC-free catheter.
A suction effect on removal may occur, probably when the catheter adheres to the bladder wall.

management.actions: Review insertion technique, catheter system, tip and coating; consider pelvic-floor exercises before insertion, relaxation during insertion and removal, UTI assessment, anaesthetic lubricant such as Instillagel, and psychological factors. Appropriate training can reduce pain.

prevention: Use PVC-free catheters for IC to reduce pain and burning.

toxicities.event: Skin lesions at the urethral meatus
recognition: Skin lesions at the urethral opening.

management.actions: Review cleansing products and additives, change disinfectants, check for fungal infection, rinse away disinfectant or lubricant residue with water, and consider dermatology referral.

toxicities.event: Lubricant sensitivity and systemic absorption of lidocaine hydrochloride
recognition: The guideline identifies allergy or sensitivity to lubricant ingredients as a safety concern.
Damaged, traumatised or bleeding urethral membranes increase the risk of systemic absorption of lidocaine hydrochloride.

management.severity: Known ingredient allergy or sensitivity, or damaged, traumatised or bleeding urethral membranes
management.actions: Do not use anaesthetic gels in these circumstances.

prevention: Check for allergy or sensitivity, including to lidocaine or chlorhexidine, before using a lubricant.

recognition: The retracted foreskin may constrict the penis behind the glans if it is not returned to position.
prevention: After catheterisation, clean the glans and penis and reposition the foreskin when present.

recognition: Excessive fluid intake and insufficiently frequent bladder emptying increase the risk of over-distension and overflow incontinence.

management.severity: Urine output > 500 ml or < 100 ml per catheterisation
management.actions: Reassess catheterisation frequency. The guideline's adaptation diagram also identifies adjustment of the interval between catheterisations and/or fluid intake.

prevention: For adults unable to void independently, IC is usually needed 4–6 times daily to keep bladder volume below 500 ml.
Perform IC shortly before sleep to limit nocturnal over-distension and sleep disturbance.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use a sterile single-use intermittent catheter to prevent cross-contamination in clinical, rehabilitation and long-term care settings.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing IC in clinical, rehabilitation and long-term care settings

prophylaxis.recommendation: Follow hand-hygiene protocols before catheterisation and teach patients and caregivers hand-hygiene techniques; patients performing self-catheterisation should clean or disinfect their hands before and after the procedure.
prophylaxis.target_population: Healthcare professionals, patients and caregivers performing IC

prophylaxis.recommendation: Clean the urethral meatus with water and pH-neutral soap.
Use hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheters for IC. The guideline cites evidence of reduced symptomatic CAUTI with ready-to-use catheters combined with a non-touch technique.
Use hydrophilic-coated catheters to prevent urethral strictures.
Use PVC-free catheters for IC to reduce pain and burning.

Advise fluid intake according to weight (25–35 ml/kg/day), fluid losses, food intake, and circulatory and renal status; encourage sufficient intake to maintain urine output of at least 1200 ml per day.

Do not routinely recommend cranberry supplementation to prevent or treat UTI; the guideline describes low-quality, contradictory evidence and states that a prophylactic effect on IC-associated infection incidence or risk has not been demonstrated.
Do not routinely use antiseptic lubricants for IC.

Assess whether bladder volume exceeds 400–500 ml, reassess catheterisation frequency when output is > 500 ml or < 100 ml per catheterisation, and perform IC shortly before sleep to prevent over-distension.
Select catheters carefully and ensure understanding of urethral anatomy and safe insertion lengths.

Check for sensitivity to lubricant ingredients such as lidocaine or chlorhexidine before use; do not use anaesthetic gels in patients with known ingredient sensitivity or damaged, traumatised or bleeding urethral membranes.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients for whom a lubricant or anaesthetic gel is considered

infection_management.prevention: Maintain appropriate catheterisation frequency and assess bladder volumes exceeding 400–500 ml; use appropriate hand hygiene and catheter technique, and consider hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheters.
infection_management.management: If an IC user has symptoms suggesting UTI, perform urinalysis or collect urine for culture. Treat symptomatic UTI only. Dipstick testing alone has limited value for ruling out infection.
Do not treat a positive urine culture without symptoms; the guideline cites antibiotic resistance and adverse effects as reasons to restrict treatment to symptomatic UTI.

infection_management.prevention: The guideline identifies infrequent IC, bladder over-distension, poor fluid intake, non-coated catheters, poor technique and insufficient education among infection risk factors.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Fungal infection associated with meatal skin lesions
infection_management.management: Check for fungal infection when skin lesions occur at the urethral meatus.

therapies_index.name: intermittent catheterisation (IC)
therapies_index.mechanism: The bladder or a urinary reservoir is drained and the catheter is then removed.
approved_indications: Acute or chronic urinary retention associated with neurogenic or non-neurogenic conditions
Overflow incontinence
Incomplete bladder emptying when residual urine causes symptoms or complications
Drainage of continent urinary diversions
Intravesical instillation, urodynamic investigations and bladder washouts
Bladder management after procedures that impair emptying
Postpartum urinary retention
therapies_index.administration: The technique and frequency depend on the setting and individual assessment. Adults unable to void independently usually require IC 4–6 times daily to keep bladder volume below 500 ml.
key_toxicities: Symptomatic urinary tract infection
Urethral bleeding or trauma
False passage
Urethral stricture
Meatal stenosis
Pain or discomfort
Rare catheter knotting and bladder perforation
Bladder or prostate calculi
monitoring: Record catheterisation frequency, drained volume and post-void residual volume.
Assess adherence, difficulties, symptoms suggesting urinary tract infection and quality of life.

therapies_index.name: clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC)
therapies_index.mechanism: The patient intermittently drains the bladder using a catheter that is removed after drainage.
approved_indications: Self-management of bladder emptying difficulties
Management of urethral stricture following the medical decision to use intermittent dilatation
therapies_index.administration: At home, non-touch technique is preferred for self-catheterisation; clean technique is used when non-touch technique is not feasible.
key_toxicities: Urinary tract infection
Urethral trauma and discomfort
monitoring: Assess the patient's ability to perform the procedure, adherence, drained volumes and reported difficulties.

therapies_index.name: intermittent urethral dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: A catheter or dilator is advanced beyond a narrowed urethral segment to maintain patency of the urethra, bladder neck or external urethral meatus.
approved_indications: Urethral stricture disease
Stenosis of the external urethral meatus
Bladder outflow obstruction
Incomplete bladder emptying
Inability to void
therapies_index.administration: Initiation follows medical advice. Patients are taught to self-dilate within a month of surgery when indicated. The catheter is ideally size 16 or 18 Ch; a smaller size may be used initially and increased if possible. Frequency may be up to daily during initial learning and subsequently adjusted to symptoms under the prescribed protocol.
monitoring: Adjust frequency according to individual symptoms and the applicable protocol.

therapies_index.name: aseptic technique
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation by healthcare professionals in ward or community settings
therapies_index.administration: Uses a sterile catheter, genital cleansing with water and soap, sterile gloves and sterile lubricant when the catheter is not pre-lubricated; sterile tweezers are optional.

therapies_index.name: non-touch technique
therapies_index.mechanism: Insertion avoids contact with the portion of the catheter entering the urethra.
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation in appropriate care settings
Preferred technique for patients performing intermittent self-catheterisation
Intermittent self-dilatation at home
therapies_index.administration: Uses hand cleansing, non-sterile gloves, genital cleansing with water and soap, and a sterile or ready-to-use catheter; a grip, sleeve or suitable package can facilitate insertion.

therapies_index.name: clean technique
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation by patients or caregivers at home when non-touch technique is not feasible
therapies_index.administration: Uses a sterile catheter, cleansing of hands and genitals, and lubricant if the catheter is not pre-lubricated.

therapies_index.name: sterile technique
approved_indications: Catheterisation in operating theatres or diagnostic situations, and for immunocompromised patients
therapies_index.administration: All materials are sterile and the procedure uses sterile gown, gloves and full operating-theatre conditions.

therapies_index.name: hydrophilic-coated catheters
therapies_index.mechanism: A water-binding coating creates a lubricated surface that reduces friction against urethral mucosa.
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation to reduce microscopic haematuria and urethral trauma
Prevention of urethral strictures
therapies_index.administration: Some products require activation with water; others are supplied ready to use.
key_toxicities: Some studies reported discomfort during withdrawal, particularly when catheterisation takes longer.

therapies_index.name: pre-lubricated catheters
therapies_index.mechanism: Lubrication reduces friction during catheter insertion and withdrawal.
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation to reduce microscopic haematuria and urethral trauma
therapies_index.administration: Supplied with lubricant already applied or provided within the packaging.

therapies_index.name: PVC-free catheters
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation to reduce pain and burning

therapies_index.name: single-use catheter
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation in clinical, rehabilitation and long-term care settings to prevent cross-contamination
Intermittent catheterisation to promote patient quality of life
therapies_index.administration: Use a new sterile catheter for each procedure in hospital and residential settings.

therapies_index.name: reusable catheters
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation when single-use catheters are unavailable, subject to local policy and applicable medical-device regulations
therapies_index.administration: Patients using them should receive instructions on cleaning, storage and lubrication under local guidelines; the guide states that evidence is lacking on effective cleaning and the number or duration of reuses.
key_toxicities: Potential contamination and cross-infection
monitoring: Review cleaning practices and adherence to local handling instructions.

therapies_index.name: non-coated catheters
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation when used with lubricant
therapies_index.administration: Lubricant should be instilled into the urethra rather than applied only to the catheter.
key_toxicities: The guide notes concerns about urethral irritation, bacteriuria and long-term urethral complications, while stating that firm supporting evidence is lacking.

therapies_index.name: micro-hole zone catheter
therapies_index.mechanism: Multiple drainage micro-holes permit bladder emptying in one flow without catheter repositioning; the guide suggests they may reduce suction.
approved_indications: Possible use when bladder emptying is incomplete

therapies_index.name: complete catheter set
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation where a connected collection bag assists urine collection or measurement
Catheterisation with limited access to suitable toilet facilities
therapies_index.administration: Usually contains a catheter connected to a urine collection bag and, when required, a lubricant or coating activator.

therapies_index.name: compact intermittent catheter
approved_indications: Intermittent catheterisation when smaller, more discreet equipment is preferred
therapies_index.administration: Sterile, single-use products available in versions for women and men; they can be used with a non-touch technique.

therapies_index.name: meatal dilators
therapies_index.mechanism: They dilate a narrowed penile urethral meatus.
approved_indications: Dilatation of the penile urethral meatus
therapies_index.administration: Available in different sizes and tip designs; the guide states that a hydrophilic coating is ideal.

therapies_index.name: lignocaine/lidocaine
therapies_index.mechanism: When supplied in lubricating gel, its local anaesthetic effect reduces procedural discomfort.
approved_indications: Anaesthetic lubrication for male catheterisation and for some women with urethral sensation
therapies_index.administration: Instilled into the urethra as anaesthetic lubricating gel when indicated.
key_toxicities: Increased risk of systemic absorption of lidocaine hydrochloride when urethral membranes are damaged, traumatised or bleeding
monitoring: Check for allergy or sensitivity before using a lubricant containing it.

therapies_index.name: chlorhexidine
therapies_index.mechanism: It is described as an antiseptic in some lubricants.
therapies_index.administration: The guide mentions its presence in some lubricants and its use for meatal cleansing, but advises against routine antiseptic lubricant use for IC.
monitoring: Check for allergy or sensitivity before using a lubricant containing it.

therapies_index.name: onabotulinum toxin A
therapies_index.mechanism: The procedures described for UUI aim to lower intravesical pressure and increase functional bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Intradetrusor injection among procedures intended to treat UUI
therapies_index.administration: Intradetrusor injection.
key_toxicities: Impaired bladder emptying and residual urine that may cause symptoms or complications requiring IC
monitoring: Assess residual urine and symptoms or complications of incomplete bladder emptying.

therapies_index.name: BCG
approved_indications: Example of an intravesical instillation for superficial bladder cancer
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation.

therapies_index.name: mitomycin C
approved_indications: Example of an intravesical instillation for superficial bladder cancer
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation.

therapies_index.name: anticholinergic medications
therapies_index.mechanism: The UUI procedures described aim to reduce intravesical pressure and increase functional bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Transurethral instillation among procedures intended to treat UUI
therapies_index.administration: Transurethral instillation is listed.
key_toxicities: The guide identifies anticholinergic medication as potentially influencing bladder emptying.
monitoring: Review medication that may affect bladder function when assessing catheterisation frequency.

therapies_index.name: cranberry supplementation
therapies_index.administration: The guide advises against routinely recommending it to prevent or treat UTI and states that evidence for prophylaxis is low quality and contradictory.

therapies_index.name: suprapubic catheterisation
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides bladder drainage through a suprapubic catheter.
approved_indications: Alternative to IC when residual urine causes symptoms or complications
therapies_index.administration: Described as an alternative drainage method, including when catheterisation is required for only a few days.

therapies_index.name: indwelling urethral catheterisation
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides continuous drainage through a urethral catheter.
approved_indications: Alternative to IC when residual urine causes symptoms or complications
Possible short-term option when circumstances make IC difficult
therapies_index.administration: An indwelling urethral catheter remains in place rather than being removed after each drainage.
key_toxicities: Compared with intermittent urethral catheterisation or suprapubic drainage, greater discomfort when drainage is needed for only a few days

therapies_index.name: male external catheter drainage system
therapies_index.mechanism: Collects urine externally.
approved_indications: May be considered for voiding problems without residual urine, symptoms or complications
therapies_index.administration: External drainage for men.

therapies_index.name: female external catheter
approved_indications: Listed as an alternative bladder-emptying method

therapies_index.name: sphincterotomy
approved_indications: Listed as a possible accompanying intervention with male external catheter use

therapies_index.name: sacral neuromodulation
approved_indications: Listed among procedures intended to treat UUI and among alternative bladder-emptying approaches
key_toxicities: The guide notes that procedures intended to treat UUI may impair complete bladder emptying and lead to symptomatic residual urine.

therapies_index.name: tibial nerve stimulation
approved_indications: Listed as an alternative bladder-emptying approach

therapies_index.name: pudendal nerve stimulation
approved_indications: Listed as an alternative bladder-emptying approach

therapies_index.name: Brindley stimulator
approved_indications: Listed as an alternative bladder-emptying method

therapies_index.name: Transobturator tape (TOT) insertion
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates some bladder outlet obstruction to reduce SUI.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for SUI
key_toxicities: Increased risk of residual urine and impaired bladder emptying
monitoring: Assess residual urine when impaired emptying causes symptoms or complications.

therapies_index.name: Tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) insertion
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates some bladder outlet obstruction to reduce SUI.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for SUI
key_toxicities: Increased risk of residual urine and impaired bladder emptying
monitoring: Assess residual urine when impaired emptying causes symptoms or complications.

therapies_index.name: Colposuspension
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates some bladder outlet obstruction to reduce SUI.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for SUI
key_toxicities: Increased risk of residual urine and impaired bladder emptying

therapies_index.name: Fascial slings
therapies_index.mechanism: Create some bladder outlet obstruction to reduce SUI.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for SUI
key_toxicities: Increased risk of residual urine and impaired bladder emptying

therapies_index.name: Bulking agents
therapies_index.mechanism: Listed with procedures intended to reduce SUI by producing some bladder outlet obstruction.
approved_indications: Listed among procedures with curative intent for SUI
key_toxicities: Procedures intended to restore continence may impair bladder emptying.

therapies_index.name: Detrusor myectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Listed with procedures intended to reduce intravesical pressure and increase functional bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for UUI
key_toxicities: Potential impaired bladder emptying and residual urine requiring IC when symptomatic or complicated

therapies_index.name: Clam ileocystoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Listed with procedures intended to reduce intravesical pressure and increase functional bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Procedure with curative intent for UUI
key_toxicities: Potential impaired bladder emptying and residual urine requiring IC when symptomatic or complicated

therapies_index.name: Mitrofanoff procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a catheterisable channel between the bladder and anterior abdominal wall to allow intermittent bladder drainage.
approved_indications: Reconstructive bladder management for conditions including bladder exstrophy or neuropathic bladder, and after cystoprostato-urethrectomy
therapies_index.administration: An intermittent catheter is passed through the channel when drainage is required.
key_toxicities: The guide reports a higher risk of bladder stones in patients performing IC through a Mitrofanoff procedure.

therapies_index.name: Monti procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses refashioned non-terminal ileum to create a catheterisable channel.
approved_indications: Construction of a channel under the Mitrofanoff principle

therapies_index.name: urinary diversion
therapies_index.mechanism: Redirects urinary drainage.
approved_indications: Alternative bladder-management method
Patients for whom urethral reconstruction is not possible or whose repair attempts have failed
therapies_index.administration: The guide gives a continent stoma and an ileal conduit as examples in the setting of unreconstructable or unsuccessfully repaired urethral disease.

therapies_index.name: urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Surgical reconstruction of the urethra.
approved_indications: Intervention considered for urethral stricture disease
therapies_index.administration: The cited Cochrane review found insufficient data to establish whether urethroplasty, urethral dilatation or endoscopic urethrotomy offers the best balance of efficacy, adverse effects and cost.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic urethrotomy
approved_indications: Intervention considered for urethral stricture disease
therapies_index.administration: The cited Cochrane review found insufficient data to establish whether this intervention, urethral dilatation or urethroplasty offers the best balance of efficacy, adverse effects and cost.

therapies_index.name: repeated sounds dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: Repeatedly dilates the narrowed urethra.
approved_indications: Urethral stricture management evaluated in a cited comparison with CISC

conditions.name: Urinary retention
conditions.description: The bladder fails to empty fully or does not empty at all. Retention may arise from neurogenic or non-neurogenic conditions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute retention involves an inability to pass urine with a painful bladder that can be felt or detected by percussion. In chronic retention, the bladder remains palpable or percussable after voiding without pain; incontinence may also occur.

subtypes.name: Acute urinary retention
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The patient cannot void and has a painful, palpable or percussable bladder; this can also occur after surgery, particularly with epidural anaesthesia.

subtypes.name: Chronic urinary retention
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A painless bladder remains palpable or percussable after voiding, sometimes with incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment of incomplete emptying and when establishing an IC schedule.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A large residual volume alone is not the basis for IC; associated symptoms or complications also matter.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure residual urine to inform catheterisation frequency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When developing an individualised IC plan.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record fluid intake, spontaneous voiding, catheterisation frequency and residual volumes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The record can inform changes to catheterisation frequency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform the catheterisation schedule using bladder volume, filling detrusor pressures and the presence of reflux.
Inform decisions about catheterisation frequency and assess urinary tract health.

follow_up.schedule: An early review is offered after IC teaching, followed by continuing support and review; no fixed interval is specified.
recommended_tests: Record of catheterisation practice and residual volumes
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Review adherence, difficulties with the procedure and its effects on everyday life.

conditions.name: Detrusor underactivity
conditions.description: Detrusor contraction has insufficient strength and/or duration, prolonging emptying or preventing complete emptying within a normal time and leaving a post-micturition residual volume. Neurological and idiopathic disorders are the most common causes described; drug therapy, including anti-muscarinic and 3 agonists, may also contribute.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Prolonged or incomplete bladder emptying with residual urine.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Residual urine may remain because detrusor contraction is inadequate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify medicines that may affect bladder function.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide identifies anticholinergic medication and ß3 agonists as examples to review.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder volume and filling detrusor pressures to guide IC frequency.

conditions.name: Bladder outlet obstruction
conditions.description: A physical blockage can prevent complete emptying despite adequate detrusor function. The guide identifies prostatic enlargement, a high bladder neck and urethral stenosis in women as common causes; urethral stricture may obstruct outflow in men.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Impaired bladder emptying and potentially symptomatic residual urine.

subtypes.name: Detrusor sphincter dys-synergia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Described as the most common cause of outflow obstruction in neurogenic bladder dysfunction: sphincter contraction is not coordinated with detrusor contraction and creates a functional obstruction.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms or complications accompanying a large residual volume, rather than the volume alone, guide consideration of IC.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The troubleshooting guidance suggests requesting this assessment for incontinence.

conditions.name: Postpartum urinary retention
conditions.description: Retention after delivery that may require IC; the guide gives a variable definition involving failure to void 6 h postpartum and a residual volume of > 150 ml.
conditions.epidemiology: May occur in up to 15% of deliveries. With prompt diagnosis, most affected patients require only temporary IC, and < 5% still need IC after 3 years. Epidural anaesthesia, episiotomy, a prolonged second stage of labour and instrument-assisted delivery increase risk.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Absence of voiding after delivery with residual urine.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The variable definition cited by the guide includes a residual volume of > 150 ml alongside absence of voiding 6 h postpartum.

conditions.name: Urethral stricture
conditions.description: An abnormal narrowing of the anterior urethra. In men, fibrosis and scarring of the urethral mucosa and adjacent spongiosus tissue narrow the affected segment. A stricture may occur at one or multiple sites. Causes identified include infection, trauma, catheterisation, intra-urethral procedures, radiotherapy, congenital abnormalities, inflammation and foreign objects; the cause may also be unknown.
conditions.epidemiology: Strictures are more common in men than women. Reported male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years, to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years, and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. In males, the bulbar urethra is the most common site (50 %), and the urethral meatus is another common site. Among men using IC, reported stricture occurrence is 4.2–25% and increases with time. A review by Liao et al. found stricture incidence of 3.1% with hydrophilic catheters and 11.5% with nonhydrophilic catheters.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Narrowing can produce obstructive voiding symptoms, incomplete emptying and other urinary complications.

subtypes.name: Female urethral stricture (FUS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: There is no universal definition. Most authors describe a fixed anatomical narrowing with reduced urethral calibre; thresholds range from < 10 Fr to < 20 Fr, with the majority using < 14 Fr, versus a normal calibre of 18-30 Fr.

subtypes.name: Bulbar urethral stricture
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A male bulbar stricture; during dilatation, the catheter is advanced into the bladder to ensure the narrowed site is crossed.

subtypes.name: Meatal strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing at the urethral opening; a meatal dilator or female-length catheter can be used for a penile meatal stricture.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If necessary when catheter insertion is difficult.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide presents degrees of narrowing by lumen calibre in French [Fr.].

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate the urethra when insertion is problematic.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If necessary when catheter insertion is difficult.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate the urethra when insertion is problematic.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If necessary when catheter insertion is difficult.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Category 0 in the cited classification denotes a normal urethra on imaging.

staging.system: European Association of Urology classification according to degree of urethral narrowing

definitions.description: Imaging shows a normal urethra; lumen and degree are recorded as –.
A subclinical narrowing leaves a lumen of ≥ 16 Fr; degree is Low.
A low-grade stricture has a lumen of 11–15 Fr; the degree cell has no entry.
A high-grade or flow-significant narrowing has a lumen of 4–10 Fr; degree is High.
A nearly obliterative narrowing leaves a lumen of 1–3 Fr; the degree cell has no entry.
An obliterative stricture leaves no urethral lumen (0 Fr); the degree cell has no entry.

follow_up.schedule: For patients prescribed intermittent dilatation, frequency may be up to daily during initial learning and subsequently reduced according to individual symptoms. The guide states that recurrence is much lower when dilatation continues for > 12 months and describes dilatation as a long-term approach unless reconstructive surgery is considered.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The location of narrowing determines how far the dilatation catheter must be advanced; it needs to pass beyond the stricture.

conditions.name: Female urethral stricture (FUS)
conditions.description: A fixed anatomical narrowing of the female urethra is the definition used by most authors, although the guide notes that no definition is universally accepted.
conditions.epidemiology: Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had undergone a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause irritative as well as obstructive voiding symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the extent of reduced urethral calibre.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When investigating a possible female stricture or difficult catheter insertion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Published definitions cited in the guide range from < 10 Fr to < 20 Fr; most use < 14 Fr as diagnostic, compared with a normal calibre of 18-30 Fr.

staging.system: European Association of Urology classification according to degree of urethral narrowing

definitions.description: The urethra appears normal on imaging; lumen and degree are –.
Subclinical narrowing with a remaining lumen of ≥ 16 Fr; degree Low.
Low-grade narrowing with a lumen of 11–15 Fr; no degree is entered.
High-grade or flow-significant narrowing with a lumen of 4–10 Fr; degree High.
Nearly obliterative narrowing with a lumen of 1–3 Fr; no degree is entered.
Obliteration with no urethral lumen (0 Fr); no degree is entered.

follow_up.schedule: When intermittent dilatation is prescribed, it may be performed up to daily during early learning and less often later according to symptoms.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: During dilatation, the catheter is passed into the bladder to ensure that it has crossed the narrowed segment.

conditions.name: Urethral meatal stenosis
conditions.description: A narrowed distal urethral opening that may be congenital or follow infection, inflammation, or open or endoscopic surgery. It is also described as a rare complication of IC.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide describes meatal stenosis after IC as rare, with only a few case series reported in the ‘90s.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Marked narrowing can impair voiding and cause incomplete bladder emptying.

conditions.name: Bladder neck stenosis
conditions.description: An abnormal narrowing at the bladder neck, most often associated with earlier surgery; the guide gives radical prostatectomy (RP) as an example of a preceding procedure.

conditions.name: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
conditions.description: An infection affecting the urethra, bladder, ureters or kidney. The guide defines UTI as bacteriuria or funguria accompanied by urinary symptoms, such as dysuria and fever, with a count of > 103 CFU/ml. It states that the definition of CAUTI applies to indwelling catheters rather than IC.
conditions.epidemiology: Among IC users with a neurogenic disorder, the reported 1-year incidence of UTI ranged from 62% to 77%; among users with a non-neurogenic disorder, it ranged from 38% to 42%. The guide notes that differing definitions and reporting periods make incidence comparisons difficult. In Welk and colleagues’ comparison during the first year after starting IC, users with a neurogenic disorder versus those with a non-neurogenic disorder had CAUTI in 54.9% vs. 38.9%, CAUTI-related hospitalisation in 11.3% vs. 4.0%, and ≥ 3 CAUTIs in 17% vs. 9.6%. Håkansson and colleagues reported pyelonephritis incidence of < 1% per patient per year among patients with neurogenic or non-neurogenic bladder.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urinary symptoms may include dysuria and fever. The guide also discusses incontinence, spasticity, lethargy, altered urine appearance or odour, bladder or kidney pain and autonomic dysreflexia in the context of differing published UTI definitions.

subtypes.name: Uncomplicated UTIs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Acute, sporadic or recurrent lower or upper UTI in non-pregnant women without relevant urinary tract anatomical or functional abnormalities or comorbidities.

subtypes.name: Complicated UTIs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: UTIs outside the uncomplicated category; the narrower description includes patients more likely to have a complicated course, including men, pregnant women and people with relevant urinary tract abnormalities, indwelling urinary catheters, renal disease or immunocompromising concomitant disease.

subtypes.name: Recurrent UTIs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Recurrence of uncomplicated and/or complicated infection at a frequency of at least three UTIs/year or two UTIs in the last six months.

subtypes.name: Urosepsis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Life-threatening organ dysfunction arising from a dysregulated response to infection originating in the urinary tract and/or male genital organs.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an IC user has symptoms suggesting a UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal findings are routine in IC users, and dipstick testing alone has limited value for ruling out infection.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an IC user has symptoms suggesting a UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For an in-and-out catheter specimen, > 100 colony-forming units (CFU)/ml is consistent with bacteriuria; the guide’s UTI definition additionally requires symptoms and gives a count of > 103 CFU/ml.

diagnostic_workup.test: UTI assessment tool for intermittent catheter users
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Structure assessment of UTI risk factors while incorporating the user’s perspective.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of IC users for UTI-related concerns.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide describes this tool as not validated.

follow_up.schedule: UTI symptoms as perceived by the patient are explored during IC follow-up; no fixed testing interval is given.
recommended_tests: Assessment of patient-perceived UTI signs and symptoms
Urinalysis or urine culture when symptoms suggest UTI
long_term_effects: Effects on social activity, duration of illness and time away from work
follow_up.survivorship_notes: In IC users, the guide advises treatment of symptomatic UTI only because antibiotics carry resistance and adverse-effect risks.

conditions.name: Bacteriuria
conditions.description: Bacteria present in urine; the guide distinguishes bacteriuria with urinary symptoms from a positive culture without symptoms.
conditions.epidemiology: Lamin and colleagues found asymptomatic bacteriuria in 50% of IC users. The guide reports acquisition of bacteriuria at 1–3% per catheterisation and states that almost all patients have bacteriuria by the end of the third week.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptomatic bacteriuria occurs with urinary symptoms such as dysuria and fever; asymptomatic bacteriuria has no accompanying symptoms.

subtypes.name: Symptomatic bacteriuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A significant bacterial count in urine accompanies urinary symptoms.

subtypes.name: Asymptomatic bacteriuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urine culture is positive despite the absence of symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For IC users when symptoms suggest UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A count of > 100 colony-forming units (CFU)/ml in a specimen obtained by in-and-out catheter is consistent with bacteriuria; culture positivity without symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guide states that asymptomatic bacteriuria does not require treatment.

conditions.name: Epididymo-orchitis
conditions.description: Epididymal inflammation that also affects the testis; epididymitis can be acute, chronic or recurrent and is often infectious.
conditions.epidemiology: In a retrospective study spanning 17 years (n=140), Ku et al. found epididymo-orchitis in 27.9% of people with spinal cord injury; it occurred significantly more often with CIC than with indwelling urethral catheterisation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute disease can cause epididymal pain, swelling and increased temperature, potentially involving the testis and scrotal skin.

conditions.name: Urethritis
conditions.description: Inflammation of the urethra with either an infectious or non-infectious origin; it is listed as a relative contraindication to IC.
conditions.epidemiology: Singh et al. and Wyndaele reported an incidence of 1–20% among spinal cord injury patients using IC.

conditions.name: Prostatitis
conditions.description: Bacterial prostatitis results from bacterial pathogens and may be acute or chronic. The guide identifies prostatitis as a possible cause of recurrent UTI and a relative contraindication to IC.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute bacterial prostatitis commonly begins abruptly with voiding symptoms and distressing, poorly localised pain, often accompanied by malaise and fever.

subtypes.name: Acute bacterial prostatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Abrupt onset of voiding symptoms and poorly localised pain, commonly with malaise and fever.

conditions.name: Haematuria
conditions.description: Blood in urine. The guide distinguishes a microscopy-defined form from blood visible to the naked eye. Bleeding may be an acute manifestation of urethral trauma during IC and is seen more often when patients begin IC.
conditions.epidemiology: Håkansson and colleagues reported bleeding at a frequency of 2.2% per year among IC users.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Blood may be detected on urine microscopy or be visible in the urine.

subtypes.name: Microscopic haematuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urine microscopy shows three or more red blood cells per high-power field (RBC/HPF).

subtypes.name: macrohaematuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Blood is visible to the naked eye from a concentration as low as 1 ml blood per litre of urine; the guide also calls this gross or frank haematuria.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The cited threshold is three or more red blood cells per high-power field (RBC/HPF).

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Significant visible haematuria is listed as a relative contraindication to IC.

conditions.name: False passage
conditions.description: A catheter or another instrument travels through the urethral wall instead of following its normal lumen. This complication of urethral trauma can prevent continued IC if the catheter repeatedly enters the false route.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide considers false passages likely to be under-reported. A scoping review by Engberg et al. reported an annual incidence of 2.2–9%, while noting limited research on prevalence and intervention.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Difficulty or inability to catheterise may occur.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: A suspected or confirmed false passage is listed as a contraindication to intermittent urethral dilatation.

conditions.name: Bladder perforation
conditions.description: A complication reported at the anastomotic site of augmented bladders.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide characterises it as rare, with sporadic reports.

conditions.name: bladder stones
conditions.description: Stone formation in the bladder. The guide associates increased risk with recurrent UTI involving urease-producing organisms, incomplete emptying, permanent catheters, immobilisation and hypercalciuria. It also links long-term IC to greater stone risk, particularly when IC is performed through a Mitrofanoff procedure.
conditions.epidemiology: Bartel et al. found bladder stones in 2% of spinal cord injury patients using IC, compared with 11% using suprapubic catheters and 6.6% using indwelling catheters. The mean period to stone development was ~10 years, and time to recurrence was 26 months.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guide suggests that pubic hair introduced during catheterisation through a Mitrofanoff procedure can provide a focus for stone formation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with acute or chronic urinary retention caused by neurogenic or non-neurogenic dysfunction who need assisted bladder emptying.
decision_rules: IC is an assisted bladder-drainage option when the patient can perform it reliably or an appropriately trained person can do so.
When the indication is a large post-void residual volume, use symptoms or complications attributable to that volume—not the residual measurement alone—to decide whether IC is needed.
Do not use IC when high intravesical pressure requires uninterrupted free drainage to prevent renal damage.
Individualise catheterisation frequency using the voiding diary, functional bladder capacity, residual-volume measurements, relevant urodynamic findings and renal function.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Drain the bladder intermittently and remove the catheter afterward. Select the technique, catheter and schedule according to the patient, care setting and local policy.

recommended_regimens.name: Hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheters
recommended_regimens.summary: Use these catheters for IC; lubrication reduces friction and urethral trauma.

alternative_regimens.name: Suprapubic catheterisation
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative for patients with residual urine accompanied by symptoms or complications.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when IC is unsuitable. For catheterisation lasting only a few days, suprapubic drainage causes less discomfort than indwelling urethral catheterisation.

alternative_regimens.name: Indwelling urethral catheterisation
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative method of bladder drainage.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when IC cannot be performed; the guide generally favours intermittent or suprapubic drainage over this option for a few days of catheterisation and with respect to symptomatic UTI.

response_assessment.timepoint: When IC is being established and during subsequent review
response_assessment.method: Record independently voided volume, volume drained by catheter, fluid intake and catheterisation frequency in a voiding diary.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the record with the patient and caregiver to determine whether the IC interval needs adjustment.

response_assessment.timepoint: At each catheterisation when urine output is > 500 ml or < 100 ml
response_assessment.interpretation: Consider changing the interval, frequency or fluid intake.

supportive_care: Provide instruction, suitable supplies and continuing support.
Encourage hand hygiene before and after catheterisation.
Advise fluid intake according to weight (25–35 ml/kg/day), fluid loss, food intake, and circulatory and renal status; encourage urine output of at least 1200 ml per day.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Urethral trauma, urethritis, prostatitis/urinary tract infection and significant visible haematuria are relative contraindications. Poor manual dexterity is a relative contraindication when no suitably trained caregiver or attendant is available.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with symptomatic or complicated incomplete bladder emptying, including those with neurogenic or hypotonic bladder or residual urine after bladder augmentation, intravesical onabotulinum toxin A injection or mid-urethral tape insertion.
decision_rules: Determine whether residual urine produces symptoms or complications before starting IC solely for a large residual volume.
Review medicines that affect bladder function, including anticholinergic medication and ß3 agonists.
Consider a micro-hole zone catheter if bladder emptying remains incomplete.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use intermittent bladder drainage when incomplete emptying warrants intervention; tailor catheter choice and frequency to the individual.

alternative_regimens.name: Micro-hole zone catheter
alternative_regimens.summary: This catheter design may assist complete emptying without repositioning.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when bladder emptying is incomplete.

response_assessment.method: Measure drained and residual urine volumes and use a voiding diary.
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust the catheterisation schedule in consultation with the patient and caregiver.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A large post-void residual volume can be accompanied by urinary tract infection, bladder calculi, renal failure, discomfort, lower urinary tract symptoms or incontinence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults whose reduced detrusor contraction strength and/or duration results in prolonged or incomplete bladder emptying.
decision_rules: Assess the residual volume and its consequences when deciding whether assisted emptying is necessary.
Account for neurological or idiopathic causes and medicines that may contribute to underactivity.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use IC when detrusor dysfunction causes incomplete emptying that requires bladder drainage.

response_assessment.method: Assess independently voided and catheter-drained volumes.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the findings to individualise IC frequency.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults whose bladder cannot empty completely because of anatomical obstruction or detrusor sphincter dys-synergia.
decision_rules: Consider IC when obstruction leads to incomplete emptying requiring drainage.
Choose the catheter and tip after assessing the patient's anatomy and circumstances.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide intermittent drainage when impaired emptying due to bladder outlet obstruction warrants catheterisation.

alternative_regimens.name: Tiemann/Coudé
alternative_regimens.summary: Its angled, tapered tip can facilitate passage through a narrow urethral passage or prostatic obstruction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when urethral narrowing or prostatic obstruction makes insertion difficult.

response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, drained volumes and any difficulty passing the catheter.
response_assessment.interpretation: If catheterisation cannot be accomplished, seek a urologist's advice.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Causes described include prostatic enlargement, high bladder neck, female urethral stenosis, male urethral stricture and detrusor sphincter dys-synergia in neurogenic bladder dysfunction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with postoperative urinary retention or impaired emptying after continence procedures, particularly when residual urine causes symptoms or complications.
decision_rules: After surgery to restore continence, determine whether residual urine is associated with symptoms or complications before initiating IC.
Consider postoperative acute urinary retention, particularly following epidural anaesthetic.
After procedures for SUI or UUI, reassess bladder emptying because the intended treatment effect may leave clinically consequential residual urine.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use intermittent drainage for postoperative retention or residual urine that causes symptoms or complications.

response_assessment.timepoint: Following surgery and while IC is required
response_assessment.method: Monitor bladder emptying, residual volume, symptoms and complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the findings to determine the need for and frequency of IC.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide identifies increased residual-volume risk after TOT, TVT, colposuspension and fascial slings. Procedures for UUI can also impair complete emptying.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with postpartum urinary retention, variably defined as no voiding 6 h postpartum with residual volume > 150 ml.
decision_rules: Identify postpartum retention promptly and use IC when bladder drainage is required.
Recognise epidural anaesthesia, episiotomy, prolonged second stage of labour and instrument-assisted delivery as factors that increase retention risk.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Manage postpartum retention with IC; most promptly diagnosed patients require it only temporarily.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guide reports faster return to normal bladder function with IC than with an indwelling catheter; < 5% still need IC after 3 years.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Temporary for most patients diagnosed promptly.

alternative_regimens.name: Indwelling urethral catheterisation
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative means of bladder drainage.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider if IC cannot be used; the guide reports faster recovery of normal bladder function with IC.

response_assessment.method: Reassess the ability to void and residual urine.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether temporary IC remains necessary.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide reports that postpartum urinary retention requiring IC may occur in up to 15% of deliveries.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with a catheterisable urinary diversion or reconstructed reservoir, including a Mitrofanoff pouch or Studer neobladder.
decision_rules: Catheterise through the constructed channel when the bladder or reservoir requires drainage.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent catheterisation (IC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use a catheter to empty the bladder, augmented bladder or reconstructed neobladder through its catheterisable channel.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide describes increased bladder-calculus risk in patients performing IC through a Mitrofanoff procedure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Users of intermittent catheterisation with symptoms suggesting UTI.
decision_rules: Investigate suspected symptomatic UTI with urinalysis or a urine specimen for culture.
Treat symptomatic UTI only; bacteriuria without symptoms does not warrant treatment in IC users.
Do not rely on a dipstick result alone to rule out infection.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of symptomatic UTI
recommended_regimens.summary: Restrict treatment in IC users to infections accompanied by symptoms; the guide does not specify an antimicrobial regimen.

not_recommended.name: Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria
not_recommended.reason: Treatment is reserved for symptomatic UTI because of antibiotic resistance and adverse-effect risks.

not_recommended.name: Routine cranberry supplementation
not_recommended.reason: The guide does not recommend it for UTI prevention or treatment; evidence concerning its effect on catheter-associated UTI is low quality and contradictory.

response_assessment.method: Perform urinalysis or collect urine for culture.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess the findings alongside symptoms rather than using dipstick testing alone to exclude infection.

response_assessment.method: Ask about the user's perceived UTI signs and symptoms.

supportive_care: Teach patients and caregivers hand-hygiene techniques and follow hand-hygiene protocols before catheterisation.
Advise sufficient fluid intake according to individual needs and encourage urine output of at least 1200 ml per day.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that the definition of CAUTI for indwelling catheters is not applicable to IC, although it also uses CAUTI when discussing infections among IC users.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with refractory urethral stricture for whom intermittent dilatation is prescribed.
decision_rules: Begin intermittent urethral dilatation on medical advice to maintain patency.
Do not perform dilatation if urethral rupture, urinary tract infection or a false passage is suspected or confirmed.
Select the catheter type and insertion distance according to the stricture's location; advance it beyond the narrowing.
Teach self-dilatation within a month of surgery when the medical decision is that it would benefit the patient.
Follow the hospital protocol and an individually prescribed frequency.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent urethral dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Use a catheter appropriate to the stricture's position for long-term intermittent dilatation. The guide identifies size 16 or 18 Ch as ideal where it can be accommodated; a smaller Charrière size may be needed initially, with an increase over time if possible.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guide states that intermittent dilatation can reduce stricture recurrence up to 68% in selected patients and that recurrence is much lower when dilatation continues for > 12 months.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Long term; during initial learning, frequency should be up to daily and can subsequently be reduced according to individual symptoms.

alternative_regimens.name: CISC
alternative_regimens.summary: In a small RCT (n=49), participants performing CISC had a statistically significant improvement in flow rate and improved QoL compared with repeated sounds dilatation.

alternative_regimens.name: Urinary diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: The guide describes diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, when urethral reconstruction is not possible or repair attempts have failed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Urethral reconstruction is not possible or previous repair attempts have failed.

response_assessment.method: Assess individual symptoms, the ability to pass the stricture and recurrence.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use symptoms to guide frequency after the initial learning period.

supportive_care: Teach dilatation using the principles applied to IC instruction.
Healthcare professionals should use an aseptic (non-touch) technique; patients performing dilatation at home should use a non-touch technique.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A Cochrane review cited by the guide found insufficient data to determine whether urethral dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty offers the best balance of efficacy, adverse effects and cost. Patients should be told that intermittent dilatation is a long-term measure unless reconstructive surgery is considered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women undertaking intermittent dilatation for urethral stricture.
decision_rules: Insert the catheter into the bladder to ensure that it has traversed the stricture.
A mirror may assist if the urethral opening is difficult to locate.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent urethral dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Choose a catheter appropriate to the stricture and pass it into the bladder. The guide states that long-term IC in women with strictures can avoid major surgery.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Long term unless reconstructive surgery is considered.

supportive_care: Offer a mirror when locating the urethra is difficult.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men undertaking intermittent dilatation for meatal, penile, bulbar or membranous urethral stricture.
decision_rules: For meatal or penile urethral strictures, a meatal dilator or female-length catheter can be used.
Use a male-length catheter for other urethral strictures.
Pass a mid-penile stricture; if passage is uncertain, advance the catheter into the bladder.
For bulbar or membranous strictures, advance the catheter into the bladder to ensure dilatation.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent urethral dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Match the dilating catheter to stricture location and advance it sufficiently to pass the narrowing.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Long term unless reconstructive surgery is considered.

alternative_regimens.name: Meatal dilator
alternative_regimens.summary: Can be used to dilate a meatal or penile urethral stricture.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A meatal or penile urethral stricture.

alternative_regimens.name: Female-length catheter
alternative_regimens.summary: Can be used for a meatal or penile urethral stricture.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A meatal or penile urethral stricture.

response_assessment.method: Confirm that the catheter passes beyond the stricture.
response_assessment.interpretation: Advance into the bladder when passage of a mid-penile stricture is uncertain and for every bulbar or membranous stricture.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults prescribed intermittent dilatation for narrowing of the external urethral meatus.
decision_rules: Start dilatation on medical advice and select a device suited to the site of narrowing.
Do not dilate when urethral rupture, urinary tract infection or false passage is suspected or confirmed.

recommended_regimens.name: Intermittent urethral dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain patency of the external urethral meatus with an appropriately selected dilating catheter.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Frequency is prescribed according to local policy; it should be up to daily during initial learning and may later be reduced according to symptoms.

decision_rules: Schedule catheterisation often enough to avoid a bladder volume > 500 ml, while also considering urodynamic findings and renal function.

special_populations.considerations: Retention requiring IC may occur in up to 15% of deliveries. It is variably defined by failure to void 6 h postpartum with residual urine > 150 ml. With prompt diagnosis, most patients need IC only temporarily; < 5% still need it after 3 years.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: IC is used to manage postpartum retention; the cited study reports a faster return to normal bladder function with IC than with an indwelling catheter.

special_populations.population: Patients after procedures for stress urinary incontinence (SUI) or urgency urinary incontinence (UUI)
special_populations.considerations: Procedures for SUI may impede bladder emptying by increasing outlet resistance. Procedures for UUI may also leave a residual volume that produces symptoms or complications.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: IC may be needed when postoperative residual urine causes symptoms or complications.

special_populations.considerations: Female urethral stricture is uncommon but may cause irritative and obstructive voiding symptoms. The short female urethra affects how far a dilatation catheter must be advanced.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For intermittent urethral dilatation, advance the catheter into the bladder to ensure it passes the stricture. A mirror may help if the urethral opening is difficult to see. Long-term IC may help women with strictures avoid major surgery.

special_populations.considerations: Male urethral strictures can occur at different sites, so catheter length and insertion depth for dilatation depend on the stricture’s location.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A meatal dilator or female-length catheter may be used for meatal or penile strictures; other strictures require a male-length catheter. Pass a mid-penile stricture, advancing into the bladder if passage is uncertain; for bulbar or membranous strictures, advance into the bladder.

special_populations.considerations: Mucosal atrophy may contribute to pain during catheter insertion or removal.

Acute, sporadic or recurrent lower (uncomplicated cystitis) and/or upper (uncomplicated pyelonephritis) UTI, limited to non-pregnant women with no known relevant anatomical and functional abnormalities within the urinary tract or comorbidities.
Complicated UTIs

All UTIs which are not defined as uncomplicated. Meaning in a narrower sense UTIs in a patient with an increased chance of a complicated course: i.e. all men, pregnant women, patients with relevant anatomical or functional abnormalities of the urinary tract, indwelling urinary catheters, renal diseases, and/or with other concomitant immunocompromising diseases for example, diabetes.
Recurrent UTIs
Recurrences of uncomplicated and/or complicated UTIs, with a frequency of at least three UTIs/year or two UTIs in the last six months.
Urosepsis
Urosepsis is defined as life threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection originating from the urinary tract and/or male genital organs.

document_sections.heading: What’s new in this update
document_sections.content: The 2024 revision updates the 2013 guideline after broad literature searches, eligibility screening and structured appraisal of new evidence. It adds 112 references. All recommendations were reassessed, unclear wording was revised, and their number was reduced from 78 to 57 to support implementation. The complications section now gives clearer definitions; the catheter-equipment section covers updated materials and designs and removes unavailable aids; and a new section examines patients’ experiences, including barriers and facilitators in daily life.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Intermittent catheterisation (IC) is presented as the best evidence-based approach to bladder management when neurogenic or non-neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction makes voiding difficult. Improved care has increased survival after spinal cord injury/disease (SCI/D), making bladder management important in rehabilitation. Urinary tract infections are described as the leading reason for rehospitalisation after SCI/D. SCDs account for 50% of patients with spinal cord dysfunction and can result, for example, from infarction, metastasis or infection. The aims are continence, prevention of urological complications, preservation of upper and lower urinary tract function, and bladder care compatible with the person’s circumstances, physical health and quality of life (QoL). The evidence includes adults needing IC once or long term because of incontinence, retention, or prostate or genital surgery. The guideline addresses indications, contraindications, equipment, nursing care, education, and urethral dilatation, including psychological and social effects. It supports practitioners already competent in IC rather than replacing anatomical knowledge, nursing principles, local protocols or individual clinical judgement. Its procedural focus is urethral IC and intermittent urethral dilatation.

document_sections.heading: 2. Role of nurses in different countries
document_sections.content: Urology nurses’ training, competencies, titles and permitted activities vary across and within European countries. Rules governing clinical guidance, catheter products and caregiver responsibilities also differ. The guideline uses nurse specialists to refer to nurses caring for people who perform intermittent catheterisation.

document_sections.heading: 3. Methodology
document_sections.content: The guideline is intended to help nurses appraise evidence-based management and apply recommendations. It is not prescriptive, and following it cannot guarantee success in every case. Professionals should make individual decisions with patients, applying clinical judgement, evidence and expertise.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Literature search
document_sections.content: A structured search examined evidence on nursing interventions for intermittent catheterisation and urethral dilatation across preparation, insertion, catheter care, materials and complications. The initial search covered database inception through 5 November 2021; the update ran through 31 July 2023. Searches were limited to human research published in English and excluded conference abstracts, protocols, editorials, letters, comments and case reports. Databases included EBM Reviews, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, OVID Medline resources and CINAHL. Earlier-edition references were used for topics not covered by search results. Additional searches were not limited by evidence level; qualitative studies were used for the patient-perspective chapter, and book chapters were used occasionally. Principal search terms concerned intermittent catheterisation, urethral dilatation, urethral stricture and urinary retention. Records were deduplicated, titles and abstracts were independently screened by two panel members, and potentially relevant full texts were independently assessed by guideline-group members.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1 Search results
document_sections.content: The November 2021 search yielded 1433 abstracts after the stated removals. Screening retained 273 for full-text availability, and 49 articles entered the guideline. The July 2023 update yielded 553 articles; 30 abstracts proceeded to full-text assessment and 17 articles were included. During article review, 45 relevant new references were found and cited. The update also retained 96 references from the 2013 edition and added 1 reviewer-suggested article judged useful. A PRISMA diagram presents the search flow.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Limitations of the document
document_sections.content: The guideline supplies standardised clinical recommendations without legal implications and is directed to practising European urology nurses and nurses in related fields. Local assessment is needed for cost-effectiveness, which is outside its scope. Patient representatives and other stakeholders did not participate in its production. The illustrated catheter-company list is not comprehensive; similar products from companies not listed may be used.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Rating system
document_sections.content: Recommendations use a system modified from the Oxford Centre for Evidence-based Medicine Levels of Evidence (March 2009). Members critically assessed identified papers, with the Chair and Vice Chair resolving disagreements. Where feasible, recommendations receive grades A–C alongside an evidence level; the tables define both scales. Literature considered practically useful but difficult to grade was assigned evidence level 4 and recommendation grade C. A low evidence level means that stronger evidence was not identified when the guideline was written; it does not indicate that an issue lacks clinical importance. Qualitative studies were all assigned level 4 because no systematic ranking was available for them. Where research was lacking, text drew on best practice; most appendix material reflects expert opinion. Evidence-based nursing decisions also incorporate clinical experience, resources and patients’ wishes.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Review process
document_sections.content: Specialist nurses, urologists from various countries and a patient-organisation representative performed a blinded review. The group revised the guideline in response and considered relevant references received after the search period. The EAUN Board and the EAU Executive responsible for EAUN activities approved the final version.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Urethral intermittent catheterisation
