document_sections.content: IC means draining or aspirating the bladder or a urinary reservoir and then removing the catheter. Because published terminology is inconsistent, the guideline specifies its own definitions for sterile, aseptic, non-touch and clean catheterisation.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Catheterisation techniques
document_sections.content: Names used for IC techniques do not always describe consistent practice. The guideline therefore defines the techniques it discusses and principally addresses aseptic technique, which it describes as the most common approach across settings.

document_sections.heading: Sterile technique
document_sections.content: A fully sterile procedure uses sterile materials, gown and gloves under operating-theatre conditions. The guideline confines it to operating theatres, diagnostic situations and immunocompromised patients. It notes that sterile intermittent catheterisation (SIC) has commonly, but incorrectly, been used to mean aseptic catheterisation.

document_sections.heading: Aseptic technique
document_sections.content: In this guideline, aseptic catheterisation uses a sterile catheter, genital washing with water and soap, sterile gloves, sterile lubricant when the catheter is not pre-lubricated, and optionally sterile tweezers.

document_sections.heading: Non-touch technique
document_sections.content: Non-touch catheterisation is an aseptic approach, generally using a sterile catheter ready for use. A grip, sleeve or packaging may enable handling without touching the insertion portion; handling only the catheter’s conus also qualifies. The described procedure includes hand cleansing, non-sterile gloves, genital cleansing with water and soap, and a sterile or ready-to-use catheter.

document_sections.heading: Clean technique
document_sections.content: Clean technique is restricted to patients or caregivers catheterising at home. It involves a sterile catheter, cleansing of hands and genitals, and sterile or non-sterile lubricant when the catheter is not already lubricated.

document_sections.heading: Hygienic technique
document_sections.content: Because hygienic technique has been used to mean either aseptic or clean catheterisation, the Working Group does not use the term.

document_sections.heading: Diagram 2. Details of different IC techniques
document_sections.content: The diagram compares sterile, clean and differently defined aseptic or non-touch techniques by environment, catheter, lubricant, gloves, catheter care, hand and genital hygiene, and permissible handling. Its note distinguishes asepsis, meaning freedom from disease-causing contaminants, from antiseptics applied to living tissue to lower infection risk.

document_sections.heading: Urethral stricture/stenosis
document_sections.content: Urethral stricture is the preferred designation for abnormal narrowing of the anterior urethra; narrowing may occur at one or several sites and cause urinary symptoms and complications. It occurs more often in men. In men, anterior stricture involves fibrosis and scarring of the mucosa and surrounding spongiosus tissue; stenosis is preferred for posterior narrowing, where spongiosus tissue is absent. Female urethral stricture (FUS) has no universally accepted definition. Most authors describe a fixed anatomical reduction in calibre, with proposed thresholds ranging from < 10 Fr to < 20 Fr; the majority regard < 14 Fr as diagnostic, compared with normal calibre of 18-30 Fr. Stricture also describes a narrowed reconstructed urethra in transgender patients despite the absence of surrounding spongiosus tissue.

document_sections.heading: Urethral meatal stenosis
document_sections.content: Meatal stenosis is narrowing at the external urethral opening. It may be congenital or follow infection, inflammation, or open or endoscopic surgery.

document_sections.heading: Bladder neck stenosis
document_sections.content: Bladder neck stenosis denotes abnormal narrowing of the bladder neck, usually associated with earlier surgery.

document_sections.heading: Dilatation
document_sections.content: Dilatation enlarges an anatomical structure beyond its current dimensions. Urethral dilatation stretches a stenotic urethral segment using semirigid or rigid dilators or balloon distention to address narrowing and improve voiding temporarily. For this guideline, IC encompasses urethral intermittent catheterisation and intermittent urethral dilatation.

document_sections.heading: Healthcare-associated infections (HCAIs)
document_sections.content: Healthcare-associated infections arise during healthcare or in a healthcare facility and first appear ≥ 48 h after admission or within 30 days after healthcare.

document_sections.heading: Haematuria
document_sections.content: Microscopic haematuria is defined as three or more red blood cells per high-power field (RBC/HPF) on microscopy. Macrohaematuria is visible to the naked eye at concentrations as low as 1 ml blood per litre of urine.

document_sections.heading: Urinary retention
document_sections.content: Urinary retention means incomplete or absent bladder emptying. Acute retention combines inability to pass urine with a painful bladder palpable or detectable by percussion. In chronic retention, the bladder remains palpable or detectable by percussion after voiding without pain; incontinence can coexist.

document_sections.heading: Post-void residual (PVR)
document_sections.content: PVR is the volume of urine remaining in the bladder after urination.

document_sections.heading: Bacteriuria
document_sections.content: Bacteriuria means bacteria in urine and may be symptomatic or asymptomatic. For a specimen obtained by in-and-out catheterisation, > 100 colony-forming units (CFU)/ml is consistent with bacteriuria. Symptomatic bacteriuria combines a significant bacterial count with urinary symptoms such as dysuria or fever; asymptomatic bacteriuria has a positive culture without symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
document_sections.content: A UTI can affect the urethra, bladder, ureters or kidneys. The guideline defines it by bacteriuria or funguria plus urinary symptoms, such as dysuria and fever, with > 103 CFU/ml. It says that the CAUTI definition concerns indwelling catheters and does not apply to IC. One table distinguishes uncomplicated, complicated and recurrent UTIs and urosepsis; another compares differing organisational definitions, symptoms and laboratory thresholds.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Indications
document_sections.content: An indications table covers acute or chronic retention of neurogenic or non-neurogenic origin, overflow incontinence, incomplete emptying, continent urinary diversions, bladder instillations and washouts, investigations, and catheterisation associated with placement of radioactive therapeutics. When IC is contemplated for a large post-void residual, symptoms or complications attributable to retained urine—not the residual measurement alone—should justify it. A further table lists complications of large residual volumes. The guideline groups causes of incomplete emptying requiring IC into four categories.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1 Detrusor dysfunction
document_sections.content: Detrusor underactivity, also termed underactive bladder (UAB), involves contraction of insufficient strength and/or duration, prolonging emptying or preventing complete emptying within a normal period and leaving residual urine. Neurological and idiopathic disorders are the most common causes; treatment with anti-muscarinic and β3 agonists may also cause it.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2 Bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: A physical outlet blockage prevents complete emptying despite adequate detrusor function. Common causes include prostate enlargement, a high bladder neck and female urethral stenosis. Male urethral stricture can also obstruct flow and often follows infection or instrumentation, including transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP); bladder neck stenosis may follow radical prostatectomy (RP). In neurogenic bladder dysfunction, the most common outlet-obstruction mechanism is detrusor sphincter dys-synergia: absent coordination between sphincter relaxation and detrusor contraction allows sphincter contraction to create a functional blockage.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.3 Postoperative
document_sections.content: Continence-restoring operations can impair emptying and create a need for IC when residual urine produces symptoms or complications. Acute postoperative retention also occurs, particularly after epidural anaesthesia.

document_sections.heading: a. Procedures for stress urinary incontinence (SUI)
document_sections.content: Curative SUI procedures seek to reduce leakage by creating some outlet obstruction, which can leave clinically significant residual urine. Residual-volume risk increases after transobturator tape (TOT), tension-free vaginal tape (TVT), colposuspension or fascial slings. The accompanying table lists procedures intended to cure SUI.

document_sections.heading: b. Procedures for urgency urinary incontinence (UUI)
document_sections.content: Procedures for UUI aim to reduce episodes by lowering intravesical pressure and increasing functional capacity. The resulting impairment of complete, efficient emptying may produce symptomatic or complicated residual urine requiring IC. A table lists the relevant procedures.

document_sections.heading: c. Other procedures (e.g., Mitrofanoff)
document_sections.content: Some reconstructive operations create a catheterisable channel for drainage of the bladder, an augmented bladder or a neobladder. The Mitrofanoff principle uses the appendix, refashioned non-terminal ileum in the Monti procedure, or rarely Meckel’s diverticulum, to connect the bladder to the anterior abdominal wall. The bladder outlet is commonly closed, while the channel’s bladder tunnel provides a valve-like effect that limits leakage during filling. IC drains the bladder as needed. Indications include bladder exstrophy, neuropathic bladder and previous cystoprostato-urethrectomy.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.4 Postpartum urinary retention
document_sections.content: Postpartum retention requiring IC may affect up to 15% of deliveries. Definitions vary; one uses failure to void 6 h postpartum together with residual urine > 150 ml. With prompt diagnosis, IC is temporary for most patients, and < 5% still require it after 3 years. Epidural anaesthesia, episiotomy, a prolonged second stage and instrument-assisted delivery increase risk. IC for postpartum retention is associated with a quicker return to normal bladder function than an indwelling catheter.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Contraindications
document_sections.content: Few contraindications are identified. An absolute contraindication is intravesical pressure high enough to require continuous unrestricted drainage to prevent renal injury. Relative contraindications include inadequate dexterity without a suitably trained helper, urethral trauma, urethritis, prostatitis or UTI, and substantial visible haematuria.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Alternatives for intermittent catheterisation
document_sections.content: For symptomatic or complicated residual urine, alternatives are suprapubic or indwelling urethral catheterisation. If drainage is needed for only a few days, suprapubic drainage and intermittent urethral catheterisation cause less discomfort than an indwelling urethral catheter. Suprapubic or intermittent catheterisation is preferable to indwelling urethral catheterisation regarding symptomatic UTI. A male external drainage system may be considered for voiding difficulties without symptoms, complications or residual urine. The table presents additional alternative emptying methods.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1 Nosocomial infection
document_sections.content: Nosocomial or healthcare-associated infections develop during healthcare and were absent on admission. Because intermittent catheters remain in the body briefly, they do not pose a biofilm-formation risk; the guideline describes a lower risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), while also calling CAUTI the most common IC complication, particularly with neurogenic disease. True infection frequency and comparative risk are hard to establish because studies differ in definitions, assessment periods, reporting and cohorts. Estimated CAUTI incidence following IC is 2.6 and 2.7 per person per year. The 1-year UTI incidence ranges from 62% to 77% in users with neurogenic disorders and from 38% to 42% in users with non-neurogenic disorders. Lamin and colleagues reported asymptomatic bacteriuria in 50% and symptomatic CAUTI in 10–15% of IC users. During the first year of IC, Welk and colleagues found higher values for neurogenic than non-neurogenic users for CAUTI (54.9% vs. 38.9%), CAUTI-related admission (11.3% vs. 4.0%) and ≥ 3 CAUTIs (17% vs. 9.6%); this suggests neurogenic disease independently increases risk. Symptomatic infections are most prevalent when residual urine at catheterisation is greater. Bladder volume should preferably stay at or below 400–500 ml; incomplete emptying increases UTI risk. Only symptomatic UTI should be treated in IC users because antibiotics carry resistance and adverse-effect risks (LE 1b; GR A). Bladder volumes above 400–500 ml should be explored in all users (LE 3; GR C). Hydrophilic or pre-lubricated catheters are associated with reduced CAUTI risk. Ye et al. reported a significant reduction in symptomatic CAUTI with non-touch technique combined with ready-to-use, preactivated hydrophilic or gel-lubricated catheters. It remains uncertain why hydrophilic catheters show lower infection incidence; proposed explanations include less pain and microtrauma, greater satisfaction and adherence, and avoidance of touching the catheter for additional lubrication. Håkansson and colleagues reported pyelonephritis incidence < 1% per patient per year in people with neurogenic or non-neurogenic bladders. A table identifies infection risk factors and their evidence levels.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2 Epididymo-orchitis
document_sections.content: Epididymitis may be acute, chronic or recurrent and is often infectious; accompanying testicular involvement is termed epididymo-orchitis. Acute disease in IC users can cause epididymal pain, swelling and warmth, potentially extending to the testis and scrotal skin. In a retrospective study lasting 17 years (n=140), Ku et al. found epididymo-orchitis in 27.9% of people with spinal cord injury. It occurred significantly more often with CIC than with indwelling urethral catheterisation.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.3 Urethritis
document_sections.content: Urethritis may be infectious or non-infectious and generally presents with lower urinary tract symptoms. Singh et al. and Wyndaele reported an incidence of 1–20% among IC users with spinal cord injury.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.4 Prostatitis
document_sections.content: Bacterial prostatitis may be acute or chronic. Acute disease typically begins abruptly with voiding symptoms and distressing, poorly localised pain, often accompanied by malaise and fever. Prostatitis can contribute to recurrent UTI.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Urethral trauma/haematuria
document_sections.content: IC-related urethral trauma, particularly in men, can produce false passages or meatal stenosis, although these are rare. Mucosal injury may lead to later stricture or infection. Bleeding into urine is an acute manifestation, seen more often when patients begin IC; Håkansson and colleagues reported bleeding at a frequency of 2.2% per year. Hydrophilic coating or pre-lubrication significantly lowers microscopic haematuria risk, but evidence does not yet support hydrophilic catheters for reducing gross haematuria. Lubrication built into the catheter or applied separately also reduces trauma. The guideline recommends hydrophilic-coated or pre-lubricated catheters for IC (LE 1a; GR A).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1 False passage
document_sections.content: A false passage occurs when a catheter or another instrument penetrates the urethral wall. It may prevent further IC because the catheter enters the passage instead of the bladder. Such trauma is probably substantially underreported. A scoping review by Engberg et al. reported annual incidence of 2.2–9%, while finding limited evidence on prevalence and intervention.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2 Urethral stricture
document_sections.content: Repeated IC trauma can narrow the urethra and cause urinary symptoms or complications. Reported stricture frequency is about 0.1–1% in women and 4.2–25% in men; occurrence in men rises over time. Liao et al. supported hydrophilic catheters for reducing strictures, reporting incidence of 3.1% among hydrophilic-catheter users versus 11.5% among nonhydrophilic-catheter users. Hydrophilic-coated catheters should be used to prevent stricture (LE 1a; GR A). If catheterisation becomes impossible, urological advice should be sought (LE 4; GR A).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3 Meatal stenosis
document_sections.content: Meatal stenosis narrows the urethral opening and, when marked, can interfere with voiding and cause incomplete emptying. It is described as rare, with only a few case series reported in the ‘90s.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.4 Bladder perforation
document_sections.content: Bladder perforation is rarely reported and has occurred at an anastomotic site in augmented bladders.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1 Catheter knotting
document_sections.content: Knotting occurs when a catheter loops around itself and its end passes through the coils. It is extremely rare and reported more often in children. Appropriate catheter selection and knowledge of urethral anatomy and safe insertion lengths may prevent it.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2 Formation of bladder and prostate stones (calculi)
document_sections.content: Recurrent UTI involving urease-producing organisms, incomplete emptying, permanent catheters, immobilisation and hypercalciuria increase bladder-stone risk. Bartel et al. reported bladder stones in 2% of patients with spinal cord injury using IC, compared with 11% using suprapubic and 6.6% using indwelling catheters; mean time to stone development was ~10 years, and recurrence occurred after 26 months. Long-term IC is associated with bladder calculi in children and adults, with greater risk when IC uses a Mitrofanoff channel. Introduced pubic hair may act as a stone nidus. Ecer et al. associated IC use in neurogenic bladder with a higher incidence of prostate calculi than non-use; CAUTI and prostatitis were identified as principal factors increasing their frequency.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.3 Pain/discomfort
document_sections.content: Pain may accompany catheter insertion or withdrawal, bladder spasm or UTI. Possible contributors to painful insertion or withdrawal include incomplete pelvic-floor relaxation, postmenopausal mucosal atrophy and inadequate lubrication. Evidence specifically addressing IC pain and discomfort is limited. Fear of pain can obstruct relaxation and learning. Suction on withdrawal may occur because the catheter adheres to the bladder wall. Johansson et al. reported significantly more burning and pain with a hydrophilic PVC catheter than a PVC-free catheter. Severe insertion pain substantially affects QoL, and suitable training can reduce pain. PVC-free catheters should be used for IC to reduce pain and burning (LE 1b; GR A).

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Catheter material
document_sections.content: Selection of single-use device materials must consider safety, function, efficiency, comfort and environmental performance. Demand for PVC-free, phthalate-free devices is increasing. The guideline states that REACH classifies phthalates as harmful and hazardous to the body and that products containing classified phthalates have required labelling under the Medical Devices Directive (93/42/ECC) since March 2010. Phthalate-free substitutes exist for some products, although developing alternatives remains technically difficult.

document_sections.heading: Polyvinyl chloride
document_sections.content: PVC is an inexpensive, durable and flexible thermoplastic used in usually single-use, transparent catheters. Different degrees of rigidity suit individual needs for stability and resistance to buckling. Plasticisers used to soften PVC are not chemically bound to it and may cause problems such as skin reactions.

document_sections.heading: Silicone
document_sections.content: Silicone is described as highly biocompatible, with reduced toxicity and tissue inflammation and resistance to ultraviolet light. Its durability and flexibility permit thin catheter walls and a relatively large drainage lumen for the external diameter.

document_sections.heading: Ethylene vinyl acetate
document_sections.content: Ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA), also called poly ethylene vinyl acetate (PEVA), combines ethylene and vinyl acetate. It has elastomer-like softness and flexibility but can be processed as a thermoplastic.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Catheter lubrication/coating
document_sections.content: Lubrication reduces friction against urethral mucosa during insertion and withdrawal. Most current catheters have a hydrophilic coating; other options include plain PVC or silicone supplied with separate gel and catheters with applied gel. Lubricants may contain lignocaine/lidocaine, chlorhexidine, both, or water and glycerine. Sterile lubricants are single-use products and opened packs must not be reused.

document_sections.heading: Hydrophilic and gel coatings
document_sections.content: A hydrophilic polymer layer absorbs and binds water up to 10 times its own weight, forming a lubricious surface that reduces urethral friction. The coating remains intact on entry and lubricates along the urethra. Available products variously require water for 30 s to activate, contain water or saline in the package, or apply a water-soluble gel as the catheter advances from its packaging. The section names examples in each category.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1 Nelaton
document_sections.content: The standard Nelaton catheter has a flexible, soft rounded tip, a straight proximal end and usually two lateral drainage eyes, often polished for comfort.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2 Tiemann/Coudé
document_sections.content: Tiemann, also called Coudé, has a slightly curved, tapered tip and up to three drainage holes. Its angled, somewhat firmer tip offers directional control and can aid insertion through a narrow urethra or prostatic obstruction.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.3 Flexible rounded tip
document_sections.content: A flexible rounded tip may traverse orifices and urethras with differing curvature or obstruction, although some patients find its flexibility harder to control.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.4 Pointed tip
document_sections.content: The compressible pointed tip has a flexible end and may assist with obstruction or dilatation because its Charrière increases along the first centimeter. A terminal ball is intended to prevent it lodging in the urethra.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.5 Introducer/protective tip
document_sections.content: The proposed purpose of a sterile introducer or protective tip is to avoid carrying bacteria from a colonised urethral segment farther into the urinary tract. The Working Group found no studies substantiating its advantages.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.6 Micro-hole zone catheter
document_sections.content: The micro-hole zone design uses more than 80 micro-holes instead of 2 or 3 drainage eyes and is described as emptying the bladder in one uninterrupted flow without repositioning. The holes may lessen bladder suction and thereby reduce microtrauma and residual urine.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.1 Size
document_sections.content: Intermittent-catheter external size uses the Charrière (Ch or CH) or French (F, Fr or FG) scale. Available sizes range from 6 to 24; common adult sizes are 10–14 for women and 12–14 for men, while stricture treatment can require larger sizes. The chosen catheter should permit free urine flow without urethral injury. Connectors are colour-coded by size.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2 Length
document_sections.content: Male and female intermittent catheters are available in approximate lengths of ~40 cm and 7–22 cm, respectively.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3 Catheter connectors
document_sections.content: Connector colours generally indicate size internationally, but manufacturers do not all follow this convention; size should therefore be checked on both package and connector. The colour chart compares catheter sizes and tube diameters.

document_sections.heading: Luer lock connector
document_sections.content: A Luer lock connector can be attached for bladder irrigation or instillation. An adapter can also join a standard catheter connection to a Luer lock.

document_sections.heading: 7.5 Catheter packaging and disposal
document_sections.content: Opening mechanisms matter when selecting products for patients with reduced dexterity. An attached collection bag can be drained through a tap or cut open before disposal with the used catheter and packaging. In community care, omitting outer packaging or ordering bulk containers may reduce packaging waste.

document_sections.heading: 7.6 Types of catheters
document_sections.content: A diagram categorises single-use, pre-lubricated, coating-activation and reusable catheter options and combinations with lubricants or collection bags. The illustrated products are examples, not a complete inventory. A standard catheter without a bag permits direct drainage into a toilet and is convenient to store, conceal and dispose of. Complete sets connect a catheter to a urine bag, facilitating residual-volume measurement and use in bed or settings without suitable toilets. Patients with reduced dexterity may find containment easier; sets support aseptic or non-touch use.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.1 Single-use catheter
document_sections.content: The catheter types discussed are available in versions for men and women.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.1.1 Single-use catheter without coating
document_sections.content: A sterile single-use catheter without coating can be paired with lubricant and is frequently combined with a standard hospital catheterisation set. Uncoated catheters are widely thought to increase irritation, bacteriuria, dissatisfaction and long-term urethral complications, but the guideline notes a lack of firm supporting evidence.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.1.2 Single-use catheter with coating or gel
document_sections.content: Sterile single-use products with hydrophilic coating or gel on the catheter or in its wrapper facilitate insertion and removal and are intended to reduce mucosal irritation relative to uncoated products.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.1.3 Catheters with sleeves or non-touch catheters
document_sections.content: A plastic sleeve or grip guides insertion without direct catheter contact. One design covers part of the catheter; another encloses it completely and can be inserted without sterile gloves or touching its surface.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.1.4 Meatal dilator /meatal dilatation catheter
document_sections.content: Meatal dilators treat narrowing at the penile urethral opening. Different sizes and tip designs exist; hydrophilic coating is preferred.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.2 Catheter systems/complete sets
document_sections.content: Many described catheters also come connected to a collection bag and retain the corresponding single-use lubrication. Their handling for non-touch use differs by product. Complete sets generally provide a catheter, drainage bag and, when required, lubricant or coating activator. They are particularly useful where toilets are inaccessible, in constrained spaces, for wheelchair users, or when catheterising while seated or lying down.

document_sections.heading: 7.6.2.1 Discrete/compact catheters
document_sections.content: Compact products are small, discreet, sterile and single-use. Several manufacturers supply female versions, while the guideline identifies only one supplier of a male compact version. Female designs suit the short urethra and are smaller than a standard writing pen; the male design is less than half the length of a standard intermittent catheter. They retain the coating or lubrication of standard-length products, can support non-touch use, and simplify carrying, storage and disposal. Dedicated collection bags may be available.

document_sections.heading: 7.7 Examples of catheters with type of material and coating
document_sections.content: The product examples were selected by an international working group from different countries, using manufacturer-supplied information. The selection is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

document_sections.heading: 7.7.1 Catheters and catheter sets (in alphabetical order company name)
document_sections.content: The tables compare named catheters and sets by dimensions, tips, materials, coatings, package features, collection bags and manufacturer. The LoFric® Dila-Cath™ product lacks drainage eyes and cannot empty the bladder; LoFric® Insti-Cath™ is described for intermittent bladder instillation with a Luer lock adapter. The Nordic Swan Ecolabel is identified as third-party certification relating to environmental requirements.

document_sections.heading: 7.7.2 Compact male catheters (in alphabetical order company name)
document_sections.content: The tables describe compact male SpeediCath® products, including a telescopic catheter and a version with an integrated sterile collection bag, together with their materials, coating and cases.

document_sections.heading: 7.7.3 Compact female catheters (in alphabetical order company name)
document_sections.content: The tables describe compact female catheter products and compare their designs, materials, coatings, dimensions, packaging and stated handling features.

document_sections.heading: 7.8 Reusable catheters
document_sections.content: Home-use studies have explored reusable-catheter cleaning methods, but cleaning effectiveness and adherence remain concerns. Reuse occurs where single-use products are poorly available; off-label reuse lacks legal support. Evidence is missing on effective cleaning and safe frequency or duration of reuse. A new sterile catheter remains the hospital and residential-care gold standard because of cross-infection risk. Current data do not convincingly establish superiority of single over multiple use across all settings; this represents insufficient reliable evidence, not proof that no difference exists. A study of reusable catheters in chronic retention is ongoing. With the optimal technique and product uncertain, clinicians should decide jointly with patients using clinical judgement and local circumstances; cost differences can matter.

document_sections.heading: 7.9 Insertion aids and help devices
document_sections.content: Accessories may improve visibility, catheter handling or insertion when patients or caregivers use clean or non-touch IC. The appendix illustrates available aids.

document_sections.heading: 8. Principles of management of nursing intervention
document_sections.content: Starting IC requires a prescription by a doctor or nurse specialist under local policy, a suitably trained nurse, appropriate materials, a comfortable place and adequate hygienic facilities. Aseptic, non-touch or clean technique should be selected according to patient and setting, including hospital, rehabilitation centre or home; privacy remains essential everywhere. Formal recommendations are to follow local policy (LE 4; GR C), assess individual circumstances before selecting catheter, tip and aids (LE 4; GR C), and protect privacy in every location (LE 4; GR C).

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Frequency of catheterisation
document_sections.content: An individual plan can use discussion of voiding problems and QoL, a voiding diary, functional capacity and bladder ultrasound to establish frequency. Adults should generally catheterise often enough to avoid bladder volume > 500 ml, while also considering urodynamic capacity, filling pressure, reflux and renal function. In a prospective cohort (n=100), adherence to prescribed frequency was associated with lower infection risk than non-adherence. Frequency should increase if urgency, motor restlessness or spasticity persists. Patients unable to void independently usually need IC 4–6 times daily to keep volume below 500 ml. Excess fluid increases overdistension and overflow-incontinence risk. Fluid mobilised from leg oedema on lying down may fill the bladder during the first few hours; IC shortly before sleep is advised to avoid sleep interruption and overdistension (LE 4; GR C). Review frequency when drainage is > 500 ml or < 100 ml per catheterisation (LE 4; GR A). Review medicines affecting bladder function, including anticholinergic medication and ß3 agonists (LE 4; GR A). A diagram shows options to adjust intervals, frequency and fluid intake when catheterised volume is < 100 ml or > 500 ml.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Residual urine volume
document_sections.content: Early in IC, monitoring drained and residual urine, including retention, helps establish suitable frequency. A voiding diary can record fluid intake, independent voiding, catheterisation frequency and residual volume. Professionals can review it with patients and caregivers to determine whether the schedule needs changing.

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Patient and caregiver assessment
document_sections.content: Although IC is described as the gold standard for assisted bladder drainage, eligibility should be assessed before it begins. The patient must be able to perform it reliably and correctly or identify another person who can. Expectations should be addressed early; support across the different aspects of a patient’s life may improve adherence. Assessment covers understanding, diagnosis and reason for IC, urinary-tract knowledge, general health, practical ability, adherence, psychological needs, motivation and availability.

document_sections.heading: Ability to understand the information
document_sections.content: At the start, some patients have difficulty remembering procedural steps or organising materials. Small adherence studies linked early mastery and short-term continuation to knowledge, perceived complexity, misconceptions and education timing. The Working Group advises that patients with low cognitive function attend training with a caregiver or healthcare provider and demonstrate the skills back to verify understanding. More than one lesson, earlier follow-up, community-nurse support or a reminder alarm may help. In one study of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), 87% learned clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC) despite differing cognitive function; men needed 2–6 training sessions and women 2–11. That study did not use written material or other aids and did not describe the catheters. Supporting the individual’s confidence and using suitable educational media, including repeatedly accessible online resources, may facilitate learning.

document_sections.heading: General health status
document_sections.content: General health should be assessed before IC instruction to identify barriers to carrying out the procedure.

document_sections.heading: Knowledge about the urinary tract
document_sections.content: Patients need basic urinary-tract knowledge. One study found that older women’s limited familiarity with their bodies complicated mastery. Caregivers’ fear of urinary injury may affect long-term adherence, so teaching should cover lower urinary-tract anatomy and function.

document_sections.heading: Ability to perform the skill
document_sections.content: Training success depends on motor, cognitive, psychological and behavioural abilities and the environment. Neurological motor impairment, reduced dexterity or sensation, and poor vision can complicate CISC. Impaired hand dexterity or catheter type does not appear to affect stricture occurrence. Women may need a mirror to locate the urethra; motivation and suitable aids can enable success. If the patient cannot undertake ISC appropriately, a trained and suitably adapted spouse, caregiver or guardian should be identified. Ease and speed matter for fitting IC into daily life, and excessive burden can lead to discontinuation. Among 160 women instructed in home ISC after pelvic reconstructive surgery, study staff contacted participants within 72 h and surveyed them after two weeks: 85% described the instructions as very easy to understand, 10.6% as somewhat easy, and 4.2% as somewhat or very confusing; 82.0% said home ISC met or exceeded expectations.

document_sections.heading: Adherence (compliance)
document_sections.content: Adherence supports health, kidney function and control of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), but can be demanding; education, emotional and psychological support, and regular reviews are important. A small study measured median self-catheterisation time, with materials ready, at 2.23 min (range 47 s to 11.5 min), without an effect of time spent on adherence. Relevant influences include anatomical and procedural knowledge, complexity, physical limitations, misconceptions, fear of harm or inability, embarrassment, resistance to an illness identity, supply availability and timing of teaching. These may lead to activity avoidance or missed IC. Supportive professional communication can help overcome initial resistance and improve adherence.

document_sections.heading: Motivation/emotional readiness
document_sections.content: Insufficient motivation is described as the most common reason for failure. Nurses should investigate needs and wishes and respond to shock or embarrassment; acknowledging emotional reactions may improve motivation, adherence, self-esteem and wellbeing. Maintaining independence can encourage acceptance. Fear of harm and low confidence may persist and undermine long-term adherence. Social life, self-image, established routines and intimacy may conflict with IC schedules: some older people avoid circumstances that impede catheterisation, while some younger people resist an illness identity.

document_sections.heading: Need for psychological support
document_sections.content: Psychological difficulties may be the greatest obstacle to learning and continuing IC. Nurses should explore practical, emotional and psychological needs and address them through communication, information and supportive attitudes. Persistent difficulties warrant referral to a sexologist or psychologist.

document_sections.heading: Performing IC outside the patient’s own home
document_sections.content: Some patients, particularly older people, worry that unhygienic facilities outside home increase UTI risk. Public-toilet layout, wheelchair inaccessibility and poor cleanliness can make correct technique difficult; education should help people manage these barriers while remaining socially active. Patients and caregivers should be encouraged to discuss psychological concerns and plan who will catheterise if the usual caregiver is unavailable. For a short interval under especially limited sanitary conditions, such as a flight, an indwelling catheter might be preferable. A medical travel document may explain supplies to customs staff and provide a clinician’s contact details. The section recommends access to suitable educational resources (LE 4; GR C); assessment of a caregiver’s health, dexterity, motivation, understanding and availability (LE 4; GR C); confirmation of patient and caregiver understanding of urinary anatomy and function (LE 4; GR C), the relevant urological condition and need for IC (LE 4; GR C); assessment of patient motivation (LE 4; GR C); consideration of supportive devices (LE 4; GR B); help overcoming initial resistance (LE 4; GR B); discussion of psychological concerns surrounding caregiver-assisted intimate care (LE 4; GR C); and advising a medical travel document for international travel (LE 4; GR C).

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Patient and caregiver assessment
document_sections.content: A medical travel document may help people who practise IC when travelling abroad: it identifies the products they carry for bladder management and provides healthcare-provider contact details for customs queries. Appendix K provides an example. Recommendations: give patients and caregivers access to suitable learning resources (LE 4, GR C); assess a caregiver’s health, dexterity, motivation, understanding and availability (LE 4, GR C); ensure they understand urinary anatomy and function (LE 4, GR C), the relevant urological condition and the reason for IC (LE 4, GR C); assess patient motivation (LE 4, GR C) and the need for supportive devices (LE 4, GR B); help overcome initial resistance (LE 4, GR B); invite discussion of psychological concerns about caregiver-performed catheterisation (LE 4, GR C); and advise patients travelling abroad to carry a medical travel document (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 8.4 Patient and caregiver education – why, who, when, where, how and what
document_sections.content: Agreed standards for teaching patients and caregivers IC are lacking. Teaching should be provided only by appropriately trained nurses. A cited consensus meeting recommended an evidence-based teaching guideline in every healthcare facility. Education aims to give patients and caregivers greater control and problem-solving ability. If a patient cannot perform IC, a suitably trained caregiver can learn it. Counselling should cover benefits, difficulties, required knowledge and skills, regular commitment and possible lifestyle changes. Partner or caregiver support during teaching may ease concerns about private circumstances, self-worth or sexual life. Patients need physical and emotional readiness; teaching strategies should accommodate their wishes, motivation and previous learning. A caregiver or professional may need to perform IC temporarily before the patient takes over. Teaching may occur at home or in hospital, with privacy protected in either setting. Educators should remain calm, encourage and reassure learners, provide feedback, let them handle equipment and discuss the steps before demonstration, and teach consistently through modelling. More than one appointment may be needed before fully informed consent is possible. Neither patients nor caregivers should feel pressured to undertake an uncomfortable procedure; cultural and religious beliefs must be respected. Appendix A provides an information checklist. Patients need spoken explanation, practical instruction, written material and an instructional video if available. Written material should preferably be noncommercial, use plain language, and include anatomical illustrations and patient experiences; it should reinforce information given verbally. Professionals should support informed choice of technique and product. Reimbursement and product availability vary between European countries; costs, local reimbursement rules, storage and possible reuse can influence choice. The potential cost and complication burden of reuse may counter its advantages. Patients should learn that food, drink and other exposures can alter urine colour or odour; Appendix J gives examples. Recommendations: ensure professionals are competent to perform and teach IC (LE 4, GR C); have an appropriately experienced nurse teach it (LE 4, GR C); tailor teaching to patients and caregivers (LE 4, GR C); use consistent methods and behavioural demonstration (LE 4, GR C); foster a supportive relationship and setting for self-management (LE 4, GR B); enable active involvement in catheter management (LE 4, GR C); allow adequate time for spoken explanation and hands-on instruction (LE 4, GR C); and reinforce spoken teaching with written information (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 8.5 Ongoing support and follow-up
document_sections.content: Incorporating IC into daily life can be difficult, so patients and caregivers need continuing support and follow-up, although a cited report states that only half receive them. Give patients professional contact details and, where available, contacts for support networks. Offer an early professional review after training to check performance and address difficulties. Record catheterisation practice to evaluate adherence. Follow-up may take place by telephone or in a clinic; community-nurse home visits may sometimes resolve problems and improve adherence. A voiding diary may support review. On discharge, provide enough catheters, any required lubricant, bags and accessories for an initial period determined by local policy. Recommendations: continue social support through consultation or telephone to improve QoL and prevent complications (LE 2a, GR B); document catheterisation practice, relevant circumstances and cessation to assess adherence (LE 4, GR C); and ask about UTI symptoms and signs as patients perceive them during follow-up (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 9. Procedures for intermittent catheterisation
document_sections.content: The chapter addresses selection of catheterisation technique, equipment and meatal cleansing, with practical procedures for professionals and patients or caregivers in the appendices.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 Choice of technique
document_sections.content: Technique selection depends on the care setting, the person performing IC and local policy. Hospital infection-control concerns have prompted calls for sterile technique. In a small study (n=36) involving people with spinal cord injury catheterised by a nurse specialist, clean IC—termed non-touch in this guideline’s rehabilitation setting—did not appear to increase symptomatic UTI. Evidence for clean technique is weak, and cross-contamination remains a concern. Professionals should use sterile technique in theatre or aseptic technique on wards and in the community. A cited European Association of Urology guideline considers aseptic technique a compromise between UTI incidence, practicality and cost. For community-based patients and caregivers, clean or non-touch IC rather than aseptic IC is considered safe and effective without an increased symptomatic UTI risk. Diagram 5 illustrates settings and techniques without prescribing one universal approach; where single-use catheters are unavailable, it indicates reusable catheters.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.1 Intermittent catheterisation by healthcare professionals and patients/ caregivers
document_sections.content: Appendices B–E and G provide male and female insertion procedures for professionals and teaching procedures for patients or caregivers. Recommendations for professional practice: follow local IC procedures (LE 4, GR C); use a sterile single-use intermittent catheter in clinical, rehabilitation and long-term care settings to prevent cross-contamination (LE 1, GR B); check sensitivity or allergy, including to lidocaine or chlorhexidine, when lubricant is used (LE 4, GR C); and do not routinely use antiseptic lubricants for IC (LE 4, GR C). The lubricant-related recommendations marked with an asterisk should also form part of patient and caregiver education.

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Choice of catheter and equipment
document_sections.content: Selection should reflect assessment of the patient or caregiver, patient preferences, disability or other limitations, ease of use and storage, costs, and local availability and reimbursement. A person may use different catheter systems for different activities. Safety concerns alone should not exclude pre-lubricated catheters when choosing a coated product. A micro-hole zone catheter may help when bladder emptying is incomplete. Hydrophilic coatings reduce insertion trauma; the cited evidence also suggests less catheter bypass and urethral irritation, with less haematuria and pain. A systematic review of real-world data associated pre-lubricated catheters with significantly fewer symptoms suggestive of UTI than hydrophilic catheters. Some studies report discomfort on withdrawal of hydrophilic-coated catheters among people who take longer to perform IC. Most of the cited literature suggests that most patients prefer coated single-use catheters for convenience, discretion, comfort, QoL and fewer UTI episodes. Uncoated catheters need lubricant. To protect the urothelium in women and men, lubricant should form an uninterrupted urethral film: placing it only on the catheter may leave vulnerable narrow areas unprotected. Lidocaine anaesthetic gel is recommended for men and may also be needed by women with urethral sensation. Anaesthetic gel is contraindicated with known sensitivity to its ingredients or damaged, traumatised or bleeding urethral membranes because systemic absorption of lidocaine hydrochloride may increase.

document_sections.heading: 9.3 Meatal cleansing
document_sections.content: Outside complete sterile technique in theatre, the meatus may be cleaned with water and soap, or with water alone if it is not visibly soiled. Studies with indwelling catheters found water as safe as antiseptic for preparing the male meatus or female vulval area; one other study found less catheter-associated UTI with chlorhexidine cleansing. Recommendations: clean the urethral meatus using water and pH-neutral soap (LE 1a, GR A); lubricate uncoated catheters for both women and men (LE 4, GR C); select lubricant or coating after comprehensive individual assessment and consideration of why IC is required (LE 4, GR C); choose a size that permits free urine drainage while limiting trauma (LE 4, GR C); and teach users of reusable catheters cleaning, storage and lubrication according to local guidelines (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 10. Documentation
document_sections.content: At the start of catheterisation, document its indication, residual urine volume, frequency, date and time, catheter type, tip, length and size, and any difficulties during the procedure. Obtain spoken or written consent beforehand and follow local documentation policy. Appendix I contains a voiding diary. Recommendations: use a voiding diary for every IC patient to assess bladder emptying (LE 4, GR C); and offer an individual care plan that takes the stated criteria, patient and caregiver lifestyles, and effects on patient QoL into account (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 11. Troubleshooting intermittent catheterisation
document_sections.content: The troubleshooting table pairs meatal skin lesions with review of cleansers and additives, possible disinfectant changes, assessment for fungal infection, washing away residues and possible dermatology referral. For urethral mucosal trauma, review catheter size and tip, insertion technique, material, coating and lubrication. For difficult insertion, blood on the catheter or urethral bleeding, check technique, lubrication, catheter characteristics and constipation; a Tiemann tip may be an alternative for women, and urethral calibration, urethral imaging or cystoscopy may be needed. For pelvic-floor or sphincter spasticity, consider breathing or coughing relaxation methods, positioning changes, a different catheter or tip, and waiting for spasticity to subside. For pain, assess technique, pelvic-floor exercises, relaxation, UTI, catheter characteristics and psychological factors; anaesthetic lubricant such as Instillagel is another listed option. For incontinence, assess UTI and catheterisation timing, review drinking and voiding records, consider temporary absorbent or drainage aids and request bladder-function assessment. Changes in urine appearance or odour prompt urine assessment and review of fluid intake, diet and medicines. Persistent problems or complications warrant medical consultation.

document_sections.heading: 12. Infection prevention
document_sections.content: UTI can restrict social activity, prolong illness and cause missed work. Bacteriuria is acquired at a rate of 1–3% per catheterisation; consequently, almost all patients have bacteriuria by the end of the third week. Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not require treatment, whereas UTI does.

document_sections.heading: 12.1 Urinalysis
document_sections.content: Abnormal urinalysis is routine among IC users, most of whom have persistent or recurrent urinary bacteria. Because test performance is uncertain, a dipstick alone has limited usefulness for excluding infection. Recommendation: when an IC user has symptoms suggesting UTI, perform urinalysis or obtain urine for culture (LE 1a, GR A).

document_sections.heading: 12.2 Fluid intake
document_sections.content: Adequate drinking dilutes urine and supports continuing drainage and flushing. Requirements depend on body size (25–35 ml/kg/day), fluid losses, food intake, and circulatory and renal status. Inadequate intake can compound infrequent bladder emptying. With urine production < 1200 ml per day, patients may void less often than intended; stagnation and distension can increase infection rates. Excessive intake increases the risk of bladder overdistension and overflow incontinence. Recommendations: tailor fluid advice to weight (25–35 ml/kg/day), losses, food and circulatory and renal status (LE 4, GR B); and encourage enough fluid for urine output of at least 1200 ml per day (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 12.3 Cranberries
document_sections.content: Evidence has not shown that preventive cranberry supplementation changes the incidence or risk of catheter-associated UTI associated with IC. Patients should be told that supporting evidence is low quality and contradictory. Recommendation: do not routinely recommend cranberry supplements to prevent or treat UTI (LE 1b, GR A).

document_sections.heading: 12.4 Hand hygiene
document_sections.content: Healthcare professionals should maintain hand hygiene to reduce cross-infection. People who self-catheterise should disinfect their hands or wash them thoroughly with soap and water before and after catheterisation. Recommendations: follow hand-hygiene protocols before catheterisation (LE 1b, GR A), and teach patients and caregivers hand-hygiene techniques (LE 4, GR B).

document_sections.heading: 12.5 Urinary tract infection assessment tool
document_sections.content: The UTI assessment tool for intermittent catheter users is intended to help professionals examine UTI risk factors systematically while incorporating users’ perspectives.

document_sections.heading: 13. Patient quality of life (QoL)
document_sections.content: IC may affect patients’ physical, psychological and emotional everyday lives and perceived QoL, as well as partners, caregivers and families. Reported positive effects include improved urinary symptoms, uninterrupted sleep, greater independence and confidence, less incontinence, improved sexual health, and fewer local peri-urethral infections, febrile episodes, stones and deterioration of renal failure. Negative effects include difficulty accommodating IC around toilets, work and travel; preparation and scheduling demands; limited hand function in men or difficulty sitting appropriately in women; severe bowel dysfunction; UTI ≥ 4 per year; urethral stricture; dependence on a caregiver; effects on family, social life and intimacy; pain, fatigue and the need to monitor time every 2–3 h.

document_sections.heading: Effects of bladder management methods on QoL in patients with neurogenic bladder
document_sections.content: The discussed bladder-emptying methods are IC, reflex triggering, indwelling catheters and suprapubic catheters. Cited studies associate IC with better urinary symptoms and QoL after short- or long-term SCI, but a recent retrospective study reported conflicting findings: surgery and indwelling catheters could reduce urinary symptoms more effectively than IC in tetra- and paraplegic patients. Long-term adherence and QoL studies are few. One recent study reported adherence up to 84% after 1 year and significantly better QoL with CIC than indwelling catheterisation. A review reported a 28% increase in ISC-Q scores with IC compared with other bladder-management approaches. Other studies found IC well tolerated, with better urinary-specific and overall QoL. In a NARCOMS Registry survey, 9397 people with MS responded (66% response rate). PDDS ≥ 3 was reported by 65%; among these respondents, 29% reported moderate-to-severe bladder disability. Overall, 12.8% reported currently needing catheterisation; IC was the most-used approach (62%), and 61.5% of these patients reported improved QoL. Recommendation: teach patients and caregivers to use IC to improve long-term QoL in patients with neurogenic bladder (LE 3, GR A).

document_sections.heading: Reasons for cessation of IC
document_sections.content: A population-based SCI study found that movement from IC to less optimal methods, including indwelling catheters, was common when IC adherence was poor. Among paraplegic patients, inconvenience, leakage and UTI were the leading reasons for stopping. Its regression analysis linked longer time since SCI to worse bladder symptoms and ≥ 4 UTIs in a year to poorer satisfaction and feelings about those symptoms. Paraplegic participants had lower QoL than tetraplegic participants, who expressed greater satisfaction and more positive feelings. An individual approach that balances complications and QoL concerns is recommended when examining adherence or treatment changes after SCI. Recommendation: explore patient QoL and complication risk to improve adherence to IC (LE 3, GR A).

document_sections.heading: QoL and safety in patients performing IC with single or reusable catheters
document_sections.content: A single-centre study found better QoL with single-use than reusable catheters and less microorganism colonisation, including some biofilm. Cited reports also associate single-use catheters with better health status and significantly higher patient acceptance. Recommendation: recommend single-use catheters to promote QoL (LE 3, GR A).

document_sections.heading: Frequency
document_sections.content: Daily catheterisation frequency strongly affects QoL. People catheterising twice daily can more readily establish a routine confined to the home and generally continue usual activities without interruption. Catheters requiring less preparation time or fewer preparation steps, and associated with less UTI and pain, may improve QoL and long-term adherence.

document_sections.heading: Sexuality and body image
document_sections.content: Few studies address sexuality or body image in IC; case reports describe negative effects. One woman described strain in her marriage when her husband performed CIC and feared hurting her; a young man reported that his sexual life had almost ceased. Self-catheterisation may impair intimacy, particularly at age < 65 years. Some patients skip catheterisations around dates or intimate encounters to avoid disclosing CISC. Recommendation: discuss sexuality and IC during assessment and, where necessary, refer to a psychologist or sexologist (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 14. Patient perspective/experience with intermittent catheterisation
document_sections.content: About 20% of people report negative feelings about catheterisation. ISC health benefits depend on adherence. People with troublesome prior symptoms may value ISC, whereas others find it intrusive and time-consuming. Being able to perform it increases independence and reduces complication risk. In a survey of 73 patients, nurses’ explanations and catheter comfort chiefly influenced product choice. Worries about self-injury and previous ISC complications are associated with low satisfaction. Common concerns involve dependence, leakage, injury, embarrassment, sex, infection, bleeding, pain and ability to maintain hygiene. Barriers include planning catheterisation, preparation and access to suitable bathrooms, and catheter type and cost. Facilitators include a positive sense of normal body image, effective instruction, continuing support when needed, and help selecting comfortable catheter gauge and length. Initial acceptance, avoidance or denial influence psychological coping. Patients describe feeling normal, controlling bladder function and remaining independent as important. Nurses should explore the individual’s daily life to support active coping and overcome adherence barriers. A small study associated practice on a low-fidelity simulator with increased patient or caregiver confidence. Recommendations: explore emotional factors affecting patients and families during IC training (LE 3, GR B), and examine patients’ everyday activities when choosing a catheter or system for use both at home and elsewhere (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 15. Intermittent urethral dilatation
document_sections.content: Urethral strictures are more frequent in men; the document relates this to differences in urethral length and shape. Possible causes are infection, trauma, indwelling or intermittent catheterisation, intra-urethral investigations or surgery, radiotherapy, congenital abnormalities, inflammation and insertion of foreign objects; a cause may remain unknown. Establishing the cause may help treatment selection and prevention of iatrogenic strictures. The European Association of Urology classification table categorises narrowing from 0 to 5 by imaging appearance, urethral lumen and degree.

document_sections.heading: 15.1 Indications
document_sections.content: Listed indications for intermittent urethral dilatation are urethral stricture disease, external meatal stenosis, bladder outflow obstruction, incomplete emptying and inability to void. The accompanying figure shows common stricture sites.

document_sections.heading: 15.2 Contraindications
document_sections.content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs. A small RCT (n=49) comparing CISC with repeated sounds dilatation reported a statistically significant improvement in flow rate and QoL among patients performing CISC.

document_sections.heading: Why
document_sections.content: Intermittent urethral dilatation aims to maintain patency of the urethra, bladder neck or external meatus and begins on medical advice. Long-term IC may allow women with strictures to avoid major surgery.

document_sections.heading: When
document_sections.content: After a medical decision in favour of dilatation, teach the patient self-dilatation within a month of surgery. The preferred catheter size is 16 or 18 Ch. A smaller Charrière may initially be necessary if a larger catheter cannot pass; increase its size over time where possible.

document_sections.heading: How long
document_sections.content: Dilatation is considered a long-term approach. Patients should understand that intermittent dilatation must continue long term unless reconstructive surgery is considered.

document_sections.heading: 15.3 Materials and procedure
document_sections.content: Materials and technique largely match IC. Teaching requires knowing where the stricture lies: the catheter must pass beyond it. Women should advance the catheter into the bladder because their urethra is short; a mirror may help locate the meatus. For men, a meatal dilator or female-length catheter can traverse meatal or penile strictures, while other sites require a male-length catheter. Pass mid-penile strictures completely; if passage is uncertain, advance into the bladder. For bulbar or membranous strictures, always advance into the bladder. Appendix F describes the procedure. Teaching principles match those for intermittent catheterisation. Recommendations: follow hospital policy on dilatation frequency (LE 4, GR C) and advise a catheter type suited to stricture location (LE 4, GR C).

document_sections.heading: 15.4 Frequency of dilatation
document_sections.content: A doctor or nurse specialist, according to local policy, prescribes frequency. During initial learning it should be up to daily; subsequently it may decrease according to symptoms. Stricture recurrence is much lower when dilatation continues for > 12 months.

document_sections.heading: 17. Appendices
document_sections.content: The appendices contain patient-information, catheterisation and dilatation procedures, supportive devices, diaries, urine-change information, a travel document and evaluation tools. Their procedural content is based largely on Working Group experience and hospital protocols or care standards rather than high-level evidence; its evidence level is mostly 4.

document_sections.heading: Appendix A — Checklist for patient information
document_sections.content: The checklist helps professionals verify that patients have been taught IC’s purpose, basic urogenital anatomy, the procedure and how technique differs between hospital, outpatient and home settings. It covers UTI avoidance, hand hygiene before and after IC, genital washing, frequency, complications, required equipment and catheter dimensions, expiry dates, available aids, catheter preparation, cleaning and safe storage of reusable equipment, disposal and obtaining supplies. Lifestyle topics include hydration, diet to avoid constipation, hygiene and exercise. Patients should recognise possible UTI signs, including dysuria, frequency or urgency, strong odour, cloudy or dark urine or blood, fever or chills, flu-like symptoms and, particularly in older adults with underlying conditions, confusion, agitation or delirium. Difficult insertion or removal also warrants attention. Teaching additionally addresses travel, professional contact details and regular follow-up to review technique.

document_sections.heading: Appendix B — Male urethral catheterisation by a health care professional – Aseptic procedure
document_sections.content: The equipment list includes a sterile pack and catheter, non-sterile gloves, sterile lubricating gel when needed, protective materials, 20 ml sterile water for a hydrophilic catheter if not prepacked, an optional specimen container, water and pH-neutral soap, alcohol hand disinfectant, and a drainage bag or sterile urine receptacle. A spare catheter and one of another or smaller size are advised. The action-and-rationale table sets out checking the indication and allergies, explaining the procedure and obtaining cooperation, protecting privacy, positioning the patient at 30° if possible, hand hygiene, preparing equipment and activating or lubricating the selected catheter. It then describes aseptic bag connection, genital cleansing, gloves and draping. For an uncoated catheter, slowly instil 10–15 ml of lubricating gel into the urethra; with anaesthetic lubricant, wait the product’s recommended 3–5 min. Gently advance the catheter until urine drains and then 2 cm farther, or to the catheter end. Do not force difficult insertion. If urine does not flow, gentle pressure above the pubic symphysis may help; keep the bag below bladder level. Withdraw slowly in centimetre steps after flow stops, pausing if drainage restarts. Discard the catheter, clean the penis and replace the foreskin to avoid paraphimosis, keep the patient dry, measure urine, obtain a specimen if required, dispose of equipment and document the indication, residual volume, date, time, catheter details, urine appearance, difficulties and patient experience.

document_sections.heading: Appendix C — Female urethral catheterisation by a healthcare professional – Aseptic procedure
document_sections.content: The equipment list includes a sterile catheterisation pack and catheter, gloves, sterile gel if needed, protective materials, 20 ml sterile water if needed for catheter activation, optional specimen container, cleansing solution, hand disinfectant and urine receptacle; an additional catheter and a different or smaller size are advised. The procedure table covers assessment and explanation, privacy, a supine position of 30° if possible, hand hygiene and preparation of equipment and catheter. After positioning, separate the labia and cleanse the outer and inner surfaces of the labia majora and minora before the meatus, using a separate swab and wiping front to back. Where tweezers are used for insertion, the specified glove step is omitted. For an uncoated catheter, instil 6 ml of gel into the urethra; if it contains anaesthetic, wait the product’s recommended 3–9 min. Advance the catheter gently until urine drains, with gentle suprapubic pressure if needed. Keep the bag below bladder level and withdraw slowly after flow ceases, pausing if urine restarts. Finally discard the catheter, cleanse and dry the patient, measure urine when appropriate, take a specimen if required, dispose of equipment and record the procedure and patient experience.

document_sections.heading: Appendix D — Male urethral catheterisation by a healthcare professional – Non-touch procedure
document_sections.content: The checklist identifies swabs, a non-touch catheter, towels and bed protection, non-sterile gloves, 20 ml sterile water if needed, sterile gel if the catheter is not prelubricated, optional specimen container, water and pH-neutral soap, hand disinfectant and urine collection equipment. It also calls for a spare catheter and another or smaller size, and refers infected or immunocompromised patients to local guidance. The procedure verifies the order and identity, checks indications and allergies, explains the process, protects privacy, positions the patient supine at 30° if possible, performs hand hygiene, prepares the catheter and cleanses the penis. Hold only the catheter cover or non-inserted end. With the penis held upright at 90°, advance gently until drainage begins and then 2 cm farther, or to the catheter end. Gentle suprapubic pressure may assist drainage; insertion must not be forced. Keep the bag below the bladder and withdraw slowly in centimetre steps, pausing whenever drainage restarts. Afterward, discard the catheter, cleanse the penis and restore the foreskin, ensure the patient is dry and comfortable, measure urine, take a specimen if indicated, dispose of equipment, perform hand hygiene and document findings and patient experience.

document_sections.heading: Appendix E — Female urethral catheterisation by a healthcare professional – Non-touch procedure
document_sections.content: The equipment checklist covers swabs, protective materials, non-sterile gloves, catheters, 20 ml sterile water or sterile gel when needed, a specimen container if indicated, cleansing solution, hand disinfectant and urine collection equipment, with spare and different or smaller catheters. The procedure confirms identity, indications and allergies; explains the process; maintains privacy; positions the patient supine at 30° if possible; and includes hand hygiene and catheter preparation. Separate the labia and cleanse from the outer labia majora toward the meatus with separate swabs, wiping from front to back. Hold only the catheter cover or non-inserted end, then advance gently until urine flows. Keep the bag below the bladder. When flow stops, slight bladder pressure may restart it; withdraw slowly in centimetre steps and pause if urine drains again. Discard the catheter, clean and dry the patient, measure urine, collect a specimen if indicated, dispose of equipment and document the indication, residual volume, urine appearance, date, time, catheter details, difficulties and review date.

document_sections.heading: Appendix F — Intermittent urethral dilatation – female and male
document_sections.content: Dilatation closely follows the IC procedure. Professionals should use an aseptic non-touch technique; patients performing it at home should always use a non-touch technique. Choose a larger Charrière than for ordinary catheterisation with professional advice; a flexible rounded or pointed tip may help. The procedure table describes preparing materials, following the physician’s catheter order, advancing beyond the stricture to the advised depth with gentle pressure if needed, and possibly using a smaller followed by a larger catheter during the same procedure. Complete the remaining IC steps and document dilatation.

document_sections.heading: Appendix G — Patient/caregiver teaching procedure for intermittent self-catheterisation – female and male
document_sections.content: ISC teaching follows the principles of professional IC with some modifications. Non-touch technique is preferred for patient-performed ISC; use clean technique if non-touch is not feasible. Professionals can advise catheter type and Charrière for the individual situation. The teaching table begins with visual and written aids, consent according to local policy, explanation, assessment of understanding, cognition, mobility, dexterity, ability and motivation, and joint choice of catheter, technique and location. Demonstrate the procedure and allow practice with models. Teach hand hygiene before and after ISC and sex-specific genital cleansing. Agree with the patient whether the first insertion will be performed by a professional or the patient; support patient insertion with verbal instruction. Remove the catheter only after emptying, withdrawing slowly and pausing if urine reappears. Demonstrate disposal, bag drainage and urine-volume recording. Allow time between practice attempts, ask the patient to explain the procedure, observe performance where applicable, and address discomfort or difficulty. Supply catheters until initial review, teach storage and troubleshooting, document the session, provide and explain a voiding diary, arrange follow-up and give professional contact details.

document_sections.heading: Appendix H — Help devices
document_sections.content: The document notes that many previously available aids are no longer available under a new European medical-device regulation. Remaining examples include leg-mounted, bed-use and cushion mirrors, which can free both hands but may also complicate catheterisation because of transport, reversed images or limited dexterity; learning without a mirror is often encouraged. A clothing holder frees both hands; Uribag permits catheterisation without a toilet and has male and female versions. KIC-System® permits an external urinary condom to be moved temporarily for penile cleansing and catheterisation before reconnection to drainage. The process can be repeated; the document states that only one urinary condom per day is needed, potentially protecting skin and reducing cost.

document_sections.heading: Appendix I — Voiding diary
document_sections.content: The voiding diary is also termed a bladder diary, input/output record or frequency-volume chart. Complete it for the agreed interval, which may be 3 days or longer; comments supply additional information to the healthcare practitioner.

document_sections.heading: Appendix J — Changes in urine due to food and medication
document_sections.content: Urine is mostly water (about 95%); its other constituents vary with food, drinks and exposures. Such causes of colour change apply whether or not a person uses a catheter. Normal urine is described as clear and straw-coloured with almost no odour. The table shows possible changes in colour or smell and potential dietary, medication and disease-related causes.

document_sections.heading: Appendix K — Medical travel document for patients
document_sections.content: The example certificate identifies a need to carry essential medical supplies and provides space for personal, product and professional-contact details. Travellers are advised to check medical-supply carriage rules for every destination or transit country with their travel agent or airline. The notice asks that essential sterile supplies not be opened or removed and directs queries to the traveller’s clinician. Its reverse-side notice is presented in Danish, Dutch, French, German, Greek, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish.

document_sections.heading: Appendix L — Questionnaires/tools for evaluating intermittent catheterisation/intermittent selfcatheterisation
document_sections.content: The appendix describes instruments addressing satisfaction, acceptance, adherence, difficulty and QoL in IC. It identifies InCaSaQ for catheter satisfaction; I-CAT for acceptance of CISC in neurological and non-neurological populations; ISC-Q for patient-reported QoL; ICAS for adherence and, in some cases, follow-up; ICDQ for CISC difficulties; USQNB-IC for symptoms grounded in the experiences of users with neuropathic bladder; and the 30-item Qualiveen for urinary-disorder-related QoL in neurological conditions. TPE-ISC is presented as a programme supporting correct ISC technique. A UTI assessment tool is intended for joint nurse–patient use to incorporate users’ perspectives into UTI management; the appendix states that this tool is not validated.
